Space-Adiabatic Perturbation Theory

Gianluca Panati*    Herbert Spohn    Stefan Teufel
Abstract

We study approximate solutions to the time-dependent Schrödinger equation i​ε​∂tψt​(x)/∂t=H⁡(x,−i​ε​∇x)​ψt​(x)i\varepsilon\partial_{t}\psi_{t}(x)/\partial t=H(x,-i\varepsilon\nabla_{x})\,\psi_{t}(x) with the Hamiltonian given as the Weyl quantization of the symbol H⁡(q,p)H(q,p) taking values in the space of bounded operators on the Hilbert space ℋf\mathcal{H}_{\rm f} of fast “internal” degrees of freedom. By assumption H⁡(q,p)H(q,p) has an isolated energy band. Using a method of Nenciu and Sordoni [NeSo] we prove that interband transitions are suppressed to any order in ε\varepsilon. As a consequence, associated to that energy band there exists a subspace of L2​(ℝd,ℋf)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\rm f}) almost invariant under the unitary time evolution. We develop a systematic perturbation scheme for the computation of effective Hamiltonians which govern approximately the intraband time evolution. As examples for the general perturbation scheme we discuss the Dirac and Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians and we reconsider also the time-adiabatic theory.

1 Introduction

Quantum theory has the remarkable feature that certain dynamical degrees of freedom may become “slaved” and thus lose their autonomous status. The origin of this phenomenon is a separation, both in space and time, into slow and fast degrees of freedom. The fast modes quickly adapt to the slow modes which in turn are governed by a suitable effective Hamiltonian. This mechanism is called adiabatic decoupling.

As paradigm we mention the motion of nuclei. The electronic degrees of freedom rapidly adjust to the state of lowest energy at given positions of the nuclei and the electronic energy band serves as effective potential in the Hamiltonian for the nuclei. This Born-Oppenheimer approximation is the basis for the dynamics of molecules and, as a consequence, also for the microscopic theory of classical fluids. There are many other examples of a similar structure. A very widely studied case are electrons moving in the periodic crystal potential, which defines the short scale. The envelope of the electronic wave function is governed by an effective Hamiltonian obtained from the Peierls substitution, in which the band energy is taken as effective kinetic energy. For an electron coupled to the quantized radiation field the photons are the fast degrees of freedom and the dynamics of the electron is governed by an effective Hamiltonian accounting for spin precession. These and other systems have been studied extensively by model specific approximate methods without realizing that they share a common structure. In fact, all the examples given can be molded into the generic form

i​ε​∂∂t​ψt​(x)=H⁡(x,−i​ε​∇x)​ψt​(x).i\varepsilon\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi_{t}(x)=H(x,-i\varepsilon\nabla_{x})\psi_{t}(x)\,. (1)

Here H⁡(q,p)H(q,p) is an operator-valued function on the classical phase space Γ=ℝ2​d\Gamma=\mathbb{R}^{2d} of the slow degrees of freedom with qq a position like and pp a momentum like variable. H⁡(q,p)H(q,p) is self-adjoint and acts on the Hilbert space ℋf\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}} of “internal” fast degrees of freedom. After quantization H⁡(x,−i​ε​∇x)H(x,-i\varepsilon\nabla_{x}) becomes the Hamiltonian of our system. To properly define it one has to specify an ordering of the operators x,−i​ε​∇xx,-i\varepsilon\nabla_{x}, for which we will adopt the Weyl quantization rule as to be explained in full detail in the Appendix. ψt\psi_{t} is a wave function on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} with values in ℋf\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}. Thus the quantum mechanical Hilbert space of states is ℋ=L2​(ℝd,ℋf)=L2​(ℝd)⊗ℋf\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}. Finally ε\varepsilon is a dimensionless parameter which controls the scale separation, ε≪1\varepsilon\ll 1.

Examples will be given in due course and we only remark that, in general, (1) is already the result of a proper identification of the slow degrees of freedom. For example, in nonrelativistic QED qq stands for the position of the electron, whereas pp is the total momentum of the electron and photons. For an electron in a periodic potential (1) is the Hamiltonian in the crystal momentum basis with xx standing for the Bloch momentum kk in the first Brillouin zone, see [PST2].

Our goal is to construct approximate solutions to (1), a task which we divide into four steps.

(i) Almost invariant subspace. The adiabatic decoupling can be traced to a spectral property of H⁡(q,p)H(q,p). It is assumed, and it can be proved in many particular cases, that for each q,pq,p the spectrum, σ⁡(q,p)\sigma(q,p), of H⁡(q,p)H(q,p) can be decomposed into a “relevant” part σr​(q,p)\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}(q,p) and a remainder in such a way that the relevant energy band {(q,p,λ)∈ℝ2​d+1:λ∈σr​(q,p)}\{(q,p,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d+1}:\lambda\in\sigma_{\rm r}(q,p)\} is separated from the remainder {(q,p,λ)∈ℝ2​d+1:λ∈σr​(q,p)c}\{(q,p,\lambda)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d+1}:\lambda\in\sigma_{\rm r}(q,p)^{\rm c}\} by a gap, i.e. by a corridor of finite width. In many cases of interest the relevant part of the spectrum consists of a single, possibly degenerate eigenvalue and the relevant energy band is the graph of a smooth function. Of course, a given H⁡(q,p)H(q,p) could have several such relevant energy bands and we suppose one of them to be singled out, e.g., through the initial condition. To the relevant energy band of HH one associates a subspace Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H} of ℋ\mathcal{H} with the property that if ψ0∈Π​ℋ\psi_{0}\in\Pi\mathcal{H}, then ψt∈Π​ℋ\psi_{t}\in\Pi\mathcal{H} up to an error which is smaller than any power of ε\varepsilon. For this reason Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H} is called an almost invariant subspace. If H^\widehat{H} denotes the Weyl quantization of HH, then [H^,Π]=𝒪⁡(ε∞)[\widehat{H},\Pi]=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\infty}), where Π\Pi is the orthogonal projector onto the closed subspace Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H}. Of course, in practice, approximations to Π\Pi are constructed, for which at order nn the error is 𝒪⁡(εn+1)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{n+1}).

(ii) Reference Hilbert space. Clearly, on Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H} the dynamics is generated by the diagonal Hamiltonian Π​H^​Π\Pi\widehat{H}\Pi, up to 𝒪⁡(ε∞)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\infty}). While properly defined, for a further analysis of the effective dynamics inside Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H} a representation in terms of adapted coordinates for the slow degrees of freedom is more powerful. We call the corresponding Hilbert space 𝒦=L2​(ℝd,𝒦f)\mathcal{K}=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{K}_{\rm f}) the reference space. By definition 𝒦\mathcal{K} is independent of ε\varepsilon. The next task is thus to construct a linear map U:Π​ℋ→𝒦U:\Pi\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{K}, which is unitary in the sense that U∗​U=ΠU^{*}U=\Pi and U​U∗=𝟏𝒦UU^{*}={\bf 1}_{\mathcal{K}}.

(iii) Effective Hamiltonian. The effective Hamiltonian is defined through h=U​Π​H^​Π​U∗h=U\Pi\widehat{H}\Pi U^{*} as operator on 𝒦\mathcal{K}. It is unitarily equivalent to the diagonal Hamiltonian, but acts on a simpler space. While hh is still a rather abstract object, it can be expanded in powers of ε\varepsilon, which is the adiabatic perturbation theory of the title. Already the lowest order approximations provide a wealth of information on the motion of the slow degrees of freedom.

(iv) Semiclassical limit. In many applications of interest the effective Hamiltonian is of a form which allows for a semiclassical analysis. The simplest situation is a relevant band which consist only of a single, possibly degenerate, eigenvalue. Then the effective Hamiltonian has a scalar principle symbol and the semiclassical analysis is straightforward.

We are certainly not the first ones to investigate approximate solutions to (1) and we have to explain which parts of the program outlined above have been achieved before and which parts are our novel contribution. In addition there have been other approaches to (1) on which we briefly comment below.

To our knowledge, the notion “almost invariant subspace” was first coined by Nenciu [Ne2] in the context of gauge invariant perturbation theory. In the context of space-adiabatic problems Brummelhuis and Nourrigat [BrNo] construct Π\Pi for the particular case of the Dirac equation and Martinez and Sordoni [MaSo] based on [So] consider Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians. The general scheme for the construction of Π\Pi is sketched in Nenciu and Sordoni [NeSo] and applied to the matrix-valued Klein-Gordon equation. Our construction is based on the one in [NeSo], but differs in a few technical details.

As in the case of Π\Pi we construct the unitary UU in several steps. First we compute order by order the formal symbol of UU, which, after quantization, gives rise to an “almost unitary” operator. Finally the almost unitary is modified to yield a true unitary exactly intertwining Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H} and 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Our method is specifically designed to deal also with problems as the Dirac equation and the Bloch electron with external magnetic fields, where the projector Π\Pi has no limit for ε→0\varepsilon\to 0, see Remark 3.2. While the specific application and the proof are new, the general idea to construct a pseudodifferential operator which is almost unitary and diagonalizes a given pseudodifferential operator has a long tradition, [Ni] Section 7 and references therein, [Ta],[HeSj]. The method of successive diagonalization is also prominent in the physics literature, for example [FoWo] in the derivation of the Pauli equation and its corrections, [Bl1] for periodic Schrödinger operators, [Bl2] for the Dirac equation, [LiFl, LiWe] for Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians.

Our central result is the expansion of the effective Hamiltonian hh. We provide a scheme which is applicable in general and work out explicitly the expansion as h=h0+ε​h1+ε2​h2+𝒪⁡(ε3)h=h_{0}+\varepsilon h_{1}+\varepsilon^{2}h_{2}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{3}). In particular, for a relevant band consisting of a single eigenvalue, h0h_{0} is the Peierls substitution and h1h_{1} contains among other things the information on geometric phases.

Since hh has, in general, a matrix-valued symbol, we discuss and apply some results on the semiclassical limit for matrix-pseudodifferential operators with scalar principal symbol. We include this part to make the paper self-contained and to demonstrate that in many cases of interest the motion of the slow degrees of freedom can be approximately described through the appropriate classical Hamiltonian flow.

Surely the reader will have noticed that our program makes no mention of the initial conditions for (1). The reason is simply that our estimates are uniform on Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H}, respectively on 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Physically this partial independence from the initial conditions is most welcome, because in general they cannot be controlled so easily. On the other hand, in the approach of Hagedorn and Joye [HaJo2] one constructs for a specific ε\varepsilon-dependent ψ0ε\psi_{0}^{\varepsilon} the wave packet t↦ψtε∈ℋt\mapsto\psi_{t}^{\varepsilon}\in\mathcal{H}, which solves (1) up to 𝒪⁡(ε∞)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\infty}) or even 𝒪(e−c/ε)\mathcal{O}(e^{-c/\varepsilon}). Hagedorn and Joye study Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonians. Periodic Schrödinger operators are considered in [GRT, DGR], who employ a related multi-scale analysis. Whereas in the other approaches the adiabatic and the semiclassical limit are taken simultaneously, both limits are clearly separated in our results. We consider this an important conceptual advantage.

To give a brief outline of our paper. In Section 2 we explain the precise assumptions on the Hamiltonian HH and construct the almost invariant subspace Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H}. The reference space 𝒦\mathcal{K} and the unitary intertwining it with Π​ℋ\Pi\mathcal{H} are explained Section 3. The central part of our paper is the expansion of the effective Hamiltonian in Section 4. In particular, we work out the expansion for Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonians including order ε2\varepsilon^{2}. We also show that by the Howland trick the standard time-adiabatic theory can be subsumed under (1). The semiclassical analysis for the effective Hamiltonian is summarized in Section 5. Last but not least, in Section 6 we discuss the Dirac equation with slowly varying external vector potentials, since it is the simplest Hamiltonian for which the full generality of our approach is needed and yields interesting physical results. In this case ℋf=ℂ4\mathcal{H}_{\rm f}=\mathbb{C}^{4} and the classical symbol has two two-fold degenerate energy bands, one for the electron and one for the positron. Thus the reference Hilbert space e.g. for the electron band is L2​(ℝ3,ℂ2)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{2}). The effective Hamiltonian is determined including order ε\varepsilon. The principal part h0h_{0} describes the translational motion through the Peierls substitution and the subprincipal part h1h_{1} yields the spin precession as governed by the BMT equation. Since the external vector potential appears through minimal coupling, the projection P⁡(q,p)P(q,p) on the electron subspace depends nontrivially on both coordinates, in contrast to Born-Oppenheimer and time-adiabatic theory, where the relevant projection P⁡(q,p)P(q,p) depends only on one of the canonical coordinates. We end the paper with some concluding remarks in Section 7 and with an Appendix reviewing some results on pseudodifferential calculus with operator-valued symbols.

2 General setting and construction of the almost-invariant subspace

Space-adiabatic perturbation theory deals with quantum systems in which it is possible to distinguish between fast and slow degrees of freedom. In particular we assume that the Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} admits a natural decomposition as ℋ=L2(ℝd)⊗\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\otimes ℋf\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}, where L2​(ℝd)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}) is the state space for the slow degrees of freedom and ℋf\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}} is the state space for the fast degrees of freedom.

As the second structural ingredient we require that the Hamiltonian is given as the quantization of a ℬ⁡(ℋf)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})-valued function on the classical phase space ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} of the slow degrees of freedom. Hence we need to consider the generalization of the usual quantization rules to the case of ℬ⁡(ℋf)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})-valued functions on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d}. This theory is well covered in the literature, see for example [Hö, Fo, Iv, GMS]. Still, for the convenience of the reader, we provide a self-contained review of the basic results in the Appendix, where we also introduce the relevant notation.

We now state the general assumptions on which the adiabatic perturbation theory will be based in the following. Let ℋf\mathcal{H}_{\rm f} be a separable Hilbert space, the state space for the fast degrees of freedom, and ℋ=L2​(ℝd)⊗ℋf\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\rm f}. The Hamiltonian H^\widehat{H} of the full system is given as the Weyl quantization of a semiclassical symbol H∈Sρm​(ε)H\in S^{m}_{\rho}(\varepsilon). We assume that H^\widehat{H} is essentially self-adjoint on 𝒮\mathcal{S}. A point in the classical phase space ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} is denoted by z=(q,p)∈ℝ2​dz=(q,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}.

The adiabatic decoupling relies on a gap condition for the principal symbol H0H_{0} of HH.

Condition (Gap)σ.{}_{\sigma}. For any z∈ℝ2​dz\in\mathbb{R}^{2d} the spectrum σ⁡(z)\sigma(z) of H0​(z)∈ℬ⁡(ℋf)H_{0}(z)\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}) contains a relevant subset σr​(z){\sigma_{\rm r}}(z) which is uniformly separated from its complement σ​(z)∖σr​(z)\sigma(z)\setminus{\sigma_{\rm r}}(z) by a gap. More precisely there are two continuous functions γj:ℝ2​d→ℝ\gamma_{j}:\mathbb{R}^{2d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} (j=±)(j=\pm) (with γ−≤γ+\gamma_{-}\leq\gamma_{+}) such that:

  1. (G1)

    for every z∈ℝ2​dz\in\mathbb{R}^{2d} the spectral component σr​(z){\sigma_{\rm r}}(z) is entirely contained in the interval I⁡(z):=[γ−​(z),γ+​(z)]\mathrm{I}(z):=[\gamma_{-}(z),\gamma_{+}(z)];

  2. (G2)

    the distance between σ​(z)∖σr​(z)\sigma(z)\setminus{\sigma_{\rm r}}(z) and the interval I⁡(z)\mathrm{I}(z) is uniformly bounded away from zero and increasing for large momenta, i.e.

    dist⁡(σ⁡(z)∖σr​(z),I⁡(z))≥Cg​⟨p⟩σ;\mathrm{dist}(\sigma(z)\setminus{\sigma_{\rm r}}(z),\mathrm{I}(z))\geq C_{g}\left\langle p\right\rangle^{\sigma}; (2)
  3. (G3)

    the width of the interval I⁡(z)\mathrm{I}(z) is uniformly bounded, i.e.

    supz∈ℝ2​d|γ+​(z)−γ−​(z)|≤C<∞.\sup_{z\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\left|\gamma_{+}(z)-\gamma_{-}(z)\right|\leq C<\infty\,.

We denote the spectral projector corresponding to σr​(z){\sigma_{\rm r}}(z) by π0​(z)\pi_{0}(z). As explained in the Introduction, one expects interband transitions to be suppressed for small ε\varepsilon. To prove such a property we need either one of the following assumptions to be satisfied.

Condition of increasing gap (IG)m.
Let HH be an hermitian symbol in Sρm​(ε,ℬ⁡(ℋf))S_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{B(H_{\rm f})}) (with ρ>0\rho>0 and m≥0m\geq 0) such that the principal symbol H0H_{0} satisfies condition (Gap)σ with σ=m\sigma=m.

Condition of constant gap (CG).
Let HH be an hermitian symbol in S00​(ε,ℬ⁡(ℋf))S_{0}^{0}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{B(H_{\rm f})}) such that the principal symbol H0H_{0} satisfies condition (Gap)σ with σ=0\sigma=0.

Note that for the case H∈S11​(ε,ℬ⁡(ℋf))H\in S_{1}^{1}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{B(H_{\rm f})}) one can show that H^\widehat{H} – the Weyl quantization of HH – is essentially self-adjoint on the domain 𝒮⁡(ℝd,ℋf)⊆ℋ\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})\subseteq\mathcal{H}. The proof is postponed to an appendix to the space-adiabatic theorem.

In analogy with the usual time-adiabatic theorem of quantum mechanics, see Section 4.4, we baptize the following result as space-adiabatic theorem. It establishes that there are almost invariant subspaces associated with isolated energy bands. In spirit the result is not new. However, to our knowledge it appears in this explicit form only recently in the literature. Brummelhuis and Nourrigat [BrNo] gave a proof for the Dirac equation, Martinez and Sordoni [MaSo] considered Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians (cf. Section 4.3) based on results from [So], and Nenciu and Sordoni [NeSo] sketched the general scheme and applied it to a matrix-valued Klein-Gordon type problem.

Theorem 2.1 (Space-adiabatic theorem).

Assume either (IG)m or (CG). Let H^\widehat{H} be the Weyl quantization of HH. Then there exists an orthogonal projector Π∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)\Pi\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}) such that

[H^,Π]=𝒪0​(ε∞)\big[\,\widehat{H},\,\Pi\,\big]=\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}) (3)

and Π=π^+𝒪0​(ε∞)\Pi=\widehat{\pi}+\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}), where π^\widehat{\pi} is the Weyl quantization of a semiclassical symbol

π≍∑j≥0εj​πjin ​Sρ0​(ε)\pi\asymp\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}\pi_{j}\qquad\mbox{in }S_{\rho}^{0}(\varepsilon)

whose principal part π0​(z)\pi_{0}(z) is the spectral projector of H0​(z)H_{0}(z) corresponding to σr​(z){\sigma_{\rm r}}(z).

The subspace Ran​Π⊆ℋ\mathrm{Ran}\Pi\subseteq\mathcal{H} is thus an almost invariant subspace for the dynamics generated by the Hamiltonian H^\widehat{H}, i.e. [e−i​H^​t,Π]=𝒪0​(ε∞​|t|)[e^{-i\widehat{H}t},\Pi]=\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}|t|), and it is associated with the spectral band σr​(z){\sigma_{\rm r}}(z). The terminology was introduced in [Ne2]. Note, however, that RanΠ\Pi is, in general, not an almost invariant subspace in the sense of [Ne2], since Π\Pi need not have a limit as ε→0\varepsilon\to 0.

Remark 2.2.

Note that the growth condition on the gap in (IG)m is stronger than one would expect from the analysis in [NeSo] or [Te1]. Indeed, in both examples a gap which is bounded globally over phase space suffices to prove uniform adiabatic decoupling also in the presence of a Hamiltonian with principal symbol increasing linearly in momentum. More general, uniform adiabatic decoupling should hold whenever (IG)m is satisfied with γ=m−ρ\gamma=m-\rho. Indeed (3) follows from the following proof with slight modifications under this weaker condition on the growth of the gap. However, this modified proof does not give π∈Sρ0​(ε)\pi\in S^{0}_{\rho}(\varepsilon), a fact we will make use of in the following. To avoid further complications in the presentation, we decided to state only the stronger result for the stronger growth condition.

Proof. We decompose the proof into two steps.

Step I. Construction of the Moyal projector

In general π0\pi_{0} is not a projector in the Moyal algebra, i.e. π0​#​π0≠π0\pi_{0}\ \#\ \pi_{0}\neq\pi_{0}. The following lemma shows that π0\pi_{0} can be corrected, order by order in ε\varepsilon, so to obtain a true Moyal projector π\pi which Moyal commutes with HH. Similar constructions appeared in the context of the Schrödinger equation several times in the literature [NeSo, BrNo, EmWe]. Our proof was strongly influenced by the one in [NeSo], but differs in relevant details, since we consider different symbol classes. It relies on the construction of the local Moyal resolvent of H0​(z)H_{0}(z). The construction of the global inverse of an elliptic symbol, often called the parametrix, is well known [DiSj, Fo, Ni].

Lemma 2.3.

Assume either (IG)m or (CG). Then there exists a unique formal symbol

π=∑j≥0εj​πjπj∈Sρ−j​ρ​(ℬ⁡(ℋf)),\pi=\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}\pi_{j}\qquad\pi_{j}\in S_{\rho}^{-j\rho}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}))\,,

such that π0​(z)\pi_{0}(z) is the spectral projector of H0​(z)H_{0}(z) corresponding to σr​(z),{\sigma_{\rm r}}(z), with the following properties:

  1. (i)

    π​#​π=π,\pi\,\#\,\pi=\pi,

  2. (ii)

    π∗=π,\pi^{*}=\pi,

  3. (iii)

    [H,π]#:=H​#​π−π​#​H=0.[\,H,\,\pi\,]_{\#}:=H\,\#\,\pi-\pi\,\#\,H=0.

Proof. We give the proof under the assumption (IG)m. The proof under assumption (CG) is simpler, since all the symbols which appear belong to S00​(ε)S^{0}_{0}(\varepsilon).

We first provide a constructive scheme for the special case where σr​(z)={Er​(z)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(z)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(z)\} is an eigenvalue, which, at the same time, proves uniqueness of π\pi in the general case. It follows basically the construction as given in [EmWe]. The reason for including this scheme is that the aim of adiabatic perturbation theory is, in particular, to give an as simple as possible recipe for explicitly computing the relevant quantities. The inductive scheme for constructing π\pi in the special case σr​(z)={Er​(z)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(z)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(z)\} is much better suited for explicit computations than the general construction which will follow later on.

Note that π0​#​π0−π0=𝒪⁡(ε)\pi_{0}\,\#\,\pi_{0}-\pi_{0}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) and [H0,π0]#=𝒪⁡(ε)[H_{0},\pi_{0}]_{\#}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) and proceed by induction. Assume that we found π(n)=∑j=0nπj\pi^{(n)}=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\pi_{j} such that

π(n)​#​π(n)−π(n)=εn+1​Gn+1+𝒪⁡(εn+2),\pi^{(n)}\,\#\,\pi^{(n)}-\pi^{(n)}=\varepsilon^{n+1}\,G_{n+1}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{n+2})\,, (4)

where, in particular, (4) defines Gn+1G_{n+1}. Thus the next order term in the expansion πn+1\pi_{n+1} must satisfy

πn+1​π0+π0​πn+1−πn+1=−Gn+1,\pi_{n+1}\,\pi_{0}+\pi_{0}\,\pi_{n+1}-\pi_{n+1}=-G_{n+1}\,,

which uniquely determines the diagonal part of πn+1\pi_{n+1} to be

πn+1D=−π0​Gn+1​π0+(1−π0)​Gn+1​(1−π0).\pi_{n+1}^{\rm D}=-\pi_{0}\,G_{n+1}\,\pi_{0}+(1-\pi_{0})\,G_{n+1}\,(1-\pi_{0})\,. (5)

By induction assumption we also have that [H,π(n)]#=𝒪⁡(εn+1)[H,\pi^{(n)}]_{\#}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{n+1}) and thus

Essential self-adjointness of H^\widehat{H}.

Since HH is an hermitian symbol its Weyl quantization H^\widehat{H} is symmetric on the invariant domain 𝒮⁡(ℝd,ℬ⁡(ℋf))⊆ℋ\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}))\subseteq\mathcal{H}. If HH belongs to S0​(ε)S^{0}(\varepsilon) then H^\widehat{H} is a bounded operator, and there is nothing to prove.

In order to prove essential self-adjointness in the case H∈S11​(ε)H\in S_{1}^{1}(\varepsilon), we use an argument of [Ro]. The proof does not exploit the smallness of ε\varepsilon and we therefore consider any ε>0\varepsilon>0. For s>0s>0 let

3 Reference subspace and intertwining unitaries

The fact that the subspace associated with an isolated energy band decouples from its orthogonal complement up to small errors in ε\varepsilon leads immediately to the following question. Is there a natural way to describe the dynamics of the system inside the almost invariant subspace RanΠ\Pi? The main obstruction for such a simple description is the fact that the subspace RanΠ\Pi depends on ε\varepsilon and is not easily accessible. Even worse, in general the limit limε→0Π\lim_{\varepsilon\to 0}\Pi does not exist, meaning that RanΠ\Pi is not even close to an ε\varepsilon-independent subspace. In order to obtain a useful description of the effective intraband dynamics we thus need to map RanΠ\Pi to an easily accessible and ε\varepsilon-independent reference subspace.

¿From the continuity of z↦H0​(z)z\mapsto H_{0}(z) and the gap condition it follows that there is a subspace 𝒦f⊂ℋf\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}\subset\mathcal{H}_{\rm f} independent of (q,p)(q,p) such that the subspaces Ranπ0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p) are all isomorphic to 𝒦f\mathcal{K}_{\rm f}. Let πr\pi_{\rm r} be the projection on 𝒦f\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}, then Πr:=𝟏⊗πr{\Pi_{\rm r}}:={\bf 1}\otimes\pi_{\rm r} (=π^r)(=\widehat{\pi}_{\rm r}) will serve as the projector on the reference subspace 𝒦:=\mathcal{K}:= RanΠr{\Pi_{\rm r}}. Of course 𝒦f\mathcal{K}_{\rm f} is highly non-unique and a convenient choice must be made in concrete applications.

Once the reference Hilbert space is fixed we next chose a unitary operator valued smooth function u0​(z)u_{0}(z) which pointwise in phase space intertwines π0​(z)\pi_{0}(z) and πr\pi_{\rm r}, i.e.

u0​(z)​π0​(z)​u0​(z)∗=πr.u_{0}(z)\,\pi_{0}(z)\,u_{0}(z)^{*}=\pi_{\mathrm{r}}\,. (17)

The existence of such a smooth map follows from a bundle-theoretic argument given at the end of this section. Again u0​(z)u_{0}(z) is not unique and must be chosen conveniently. We will see in Section 6 that there is an optimal choice for u0​(z)u_{0}(z), which reflects the physics of the problem.

We cannot prove that it is possible to choose u0u_{0} in Sρ0​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))S_{\rho}^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})). Indeed, relation (17) does not imply any bound at infinity on the derivatives of u0u_{0}, as can be seen by multiplying u0u_{0} with a highly oscillating phase. Hence we assume that u0u_{0} is in Sρ0​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))S_{\rho}^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})), as will be the case in the physical examples.

In the following 𝒰⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}) will denote the group of unitary operators over ℋ\mathcal{H}.

Theorem 3.1.

Assume either (IG)m or (CG) and that there exists a 𝒰⁡(ℋf)\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})-valued map u0∈Sρ0​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))u_{0}\in S_{\rho}^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) which satisfies (17). Then there exist a unitary operator U∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)U\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}) such that

U​Π​U∗=ΠrU\,\Pi\,U^{*}={\Pi_{\rm r}} (18)

and U=u^+𝒪0​(ε∞)U=\widehat{u}+\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}), where u≍∑j≥0εj​uju\asymp\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}u_{j} in Sρ0​(ε)S_{\rho}^{0}(\varepsilon) with principal symbol u0u_{0}.

Remark 3.2.

In [NeSo] the Nagy transformation (22) is used in order to map RanΠ\Pi to the ε\varepsilon-independent subspace Ranπ^0\widehat{\pi}_{0}. This is possible because in their application the symbol π0\pi_{0} depends only on qq and, as a consequence, π^0\widehat{\pi}_{0} is a projector satisfying ‖Π−π^0‖=𝒪⁡(ε)\|\Pi-\widehat{\pi}_{0}\|=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon). However, in general π0\pi_{0} depends on qq and pp, see Section 6 and [PST2] for relevant examples, and the mapping to the reference space becomes more subtle.

Proof. Step I. Construction of the Moyal unitaries.

Again u0u_{0} fails to be a Moyal unitary (i.e. u0∗​#​u0≠1u_{0}^{*}\,\#\,u_{0}\neq 1) and to intertwine π\pi and πr\pi_{\mathrm{r}}. However, the following lemma shows that u0u_{0} can be corrected order by order to reach this goal. The idea of constructing a pseudodifferential operator which is almost unitary and diagonalizes a given pseudodifferential operator has a long tradition, cf. [Ni] Section 7 and references therein, and was applied in different settings many times, e.g. [Ta, HeSj].

Lemma 3.3.

Assume either (IG)m or (CG) and that there exists a 𝒰⁡(ℋf)\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})-valued map u0∈Sρ0​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))u_{0}\in S_{\rho}^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) which satisfies (17). Then there is a formal symbol u=∑j≥0εj​uju=\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}u_{j}, with uj∈Sρ−j​ρ​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))u_{j}\in S_{\rho}^{-j\rho}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})), such that

  1. (i)

    u​#​π​#​u∗=πru\,\#\,\,\pi\,\#\,u^{*}=\pi_{\mathrm{r}} ,

where π\pi is the Moyal projector constructed in Lemma 2.3.

We emphasize that – as opposed to the Moyal projector π\pi appearing in Lemma 2.3 – the Moyal unitary uu is highly non-unique even for fixed u0u_{0}. As it will follow from the proof, all the possible choices of Moyal unitaries intertwining π\pi and πr\pi_{\mathrm{r}} with prescribed principal symbol u0u_{0} are parametrized by the antihermitian Moyal symbols which are diagonal in the πr\pi_{\mathrm{r}}-splitting.

Step II. Quantization

Now let uu denote a resummation of the formal power series u=∑j≥0εj​uju=\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}u_{j} in Sρ0​(ε)S_{\rho}^{0}(\varepsilon) (see Prop. A.8). Then, by Weyl quantization, one gets a bounded operator u^∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)\widehat{u}\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}) (see Prop. A.3) such that:

  1. (i)

    u^∗​u^=1+𝒪−∞​(ε∞)\widehat{u}^{\,*}\widehat{u}=1+\mathcal{O}_{-\infty}(\varepsilon^{\infty})\qquadand  u^​u^∗=1+𝒪−∞​(ε∞)\widehat{u}\,\widehat{u}^{\,*}=1+\mathcal{O}_{-\infty}(\varepsilon^{\infty})

    u^​π^​u^∗=Πr+𝒪−∞​(ε∞)\widehat{u}\,\widehat{\pi}\,\widehat{u}^{\,*}={\Pi_{\rm r}}+\mathcal{O}_{-\infty}(\varepsilon^{\infty}).

As a first step we modify u^\widehat{u} by an 𝒪0​(ε∞)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty})-term in order to get a true unitary operator U~∈𝒰⁡(ℋ)\widetilde{U}\in\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}) (which, in general, does not correspond to the Weyl quantization of any semiclassical symbol). Let

U~=u^​(u^∗​u^)−12.\widetilde{U}=\widehat{u}\,\left(\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,\widehat{u}\right)^{-\frac{1}{2}}\,. (21)

Notice that u^∗​u^\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,\widehat{u} is a self-adjoint positive operator which is 𝒪0​(ε∞)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty})-close to the identity operator. Then (u^∗​u^)−12(\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,\widehat{u})^{-\frac{1}{2}} is well-defined and again 𝒪0​(ε∞)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty})-close to the identity operator. Hence (21) defines a unitary operator which moreover is 𝒪0​(ε∞)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty})-close to u^\widehat{u}.

Finally we modify U~\widetilde{U} in order to obtain a unitary which exactly intertwines Πr{\Pi_{\rm r}} and Π\Pi. Since ‖U~​Π​U~∗−Πr‖<1\|\widetilde{U}\,\Pi\,\widetilde{U}^{\,*}-{\Pi_{\rm r}}\|<1 for ε\varepsilon sufficiently small, the Nagy formula as used in [NeSo]

W:=[1−(U~​Π​U~∗−Πr)2]−12​[U~​Π​U~∗​Πr+(1−U~​Π​U~∗)​(1−Πr)]W:=\left[1-\left(\widetilde{U}\,\Pi\,\widetilde{U}^{\,*}-{\Pi_{\rm r}}\right)^{2}\right]^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left[\widetilde{U}\,\Pi\,\widetilde{U}^{\,*}\,{\Pi_{\rm r}}+(1-\widetilde{U}\,\Pi\,\widetilde{U}^{\,*})(1-{\Pi_{\rm r}})\right] (22)

defines a unitary operator W∈𝒰⁡(ℋ)W\in\mathcal{U}(\mathcal{H}) such that W​U~​Π​U~∗​W∗=ΠrW\,\widetilde{U}\,\Pi\,\widetilde{U}^{\,*}\,W^{*}={\Pi_{\rm r}} and W=𝟏+𝒪0​(ε∞)W={\bf 1}+\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}). Thus by defining U=W​U~U=W\,\widetilde{U} one obtains (18), with the desired properties. ∎

Remark 3.5.

We sketch how to prove the existence of a smooth map u0u_{0} satisfying (17). Given

E={(z,ψ)∈ℝ2​d×ℋf:ψ∈Ran​π0​(z)}E=\left\{(z,\psi)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}\times\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}:\psi\in\mathrm{Ran}\pi_{0}(z)\right\}

the map ΠE:E→ℝ2​d,\Pi_{E}:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{2d}, (z,ψ)↦z(z,\psi)\mapsto z defines a fibration of Hilbert spaces over the base space ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d}.

The fibration is locally trivial. Indeed for any z0∈ℝ2​dz_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{2d} there exists a neighborhood 𝒰z0\mathcal{U}_{z_{0}} such that ‖π0​(z)−π0​(z0)‖<1\left\|\pi_{0}(z)-\pi_{0}(z_{0})\right\|<1 for any z∈𝒰z0z\in\mathcal{U}_{z_{0}}, so that the Nagy formula

w⁡(z)=[1−(π0​(z)−π0​(z0))2]−12​[π0​(z)​π0​(z0)+(1−π0​(z))​(1−π0​(z0))]w(z)=\left[1-\left(\pi_{0}(z)-\pi_{0}(z_{0})\right)^{2}\right]^{-\frac{1}{2}}\left[\pi_{0}(z)\pi_{0}(z_{0})+(1-\pi_{0}(z))(1-\pi_{0}(z_{0}))\right]

locally defines a unitary operator w⁡(z)w(z) such that w​(z)∗​π0​(z)​w​(z)=π0​(z0)w(z)^{*}\pi_{0}(z)w(z)=\pi_{0}(z_{0}). A local trivialization of the fibration is then explicitly given by

Θ:ΠE−1​(𝒰z0)→𝒰z0×Ran​π​(z0)→𝒰z0×𝒦f(z,ψ)↦(z,w⁡(z)​ψ)↦(z,ϕ⁡(z0)​w​(z)​ψ)\begin{array}[]{cccccc}\Theta:&\Pi_{E}^{-1}(\mathcal{U}_{z_{0}})&\rightarrow&\mathcal{U}_{z_{0}}\times\mathrm{Ran}\pi(z_{0})&\rightarrow&\mathcal{U}_{z_{0}}\times\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}\\ &(z,\psi)&\mapsto&(z,w(z)\psi)&\mapsto&(z,\phi(z_{0})w(z)\psi)\end{array}

where we use the fact that there exists a unitary operator ϕ⁡(z0):Ran​π​(z0)→𝒦f\phi(z_{0}):\mathrm{Ran}\pi(z_{0})\rightarrow\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}. The existence of ϕ⁡(z0)\phi(z_{0}) follows from the fact that the dimension of Ran​π​(z0)\mathrm{Ran}\pi(z_{0}) is independent of z0z_{0}, but the map z0↦ϕ⁡(z0)z_{0}\mapsto\phi(z_{0}) may be a priori even discontinuous.

Moreover one can check that any two such trivializations are 𝒰⁡(𝒦f)\mathcal{U(K}_{\mathrm{f}})-compatible, and the previous data define a linear 𝒰⁡(𝒦f)\mathcal{U(K}_{\mathrm{f}})-bundle.

Since the base space is contractible, the bundle is trivial and the associated principal 𝒰⁡(𝒦f)\mathcal{U(K}_{\mathrm{f}})-bundle (i.e. the bundle of the orthonormal frames) admits a global smooth section. This implies the existence of a smooth map u0:u_{0}: ℝ2​d→𝒰⁡(ℋf)\mathbb{R}^{2d}\rightarrow\mathcal{U(H}_{\mathrm{f}}) such that (17) holds true.

4 Adiabatic perturbation theory

4.1 The effective Hamiltonian

In the previous section we constructed a unitary UU on ℋ\mathcal{H} which exactly intertwines the almost invariant subspace RanΠ\Pi and the reference subspace 𝒦=\mathcal{K}= RanΠr{\Pi_{\rm r}}. UU and Π\Pi are 𝒪0​(ε∞)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty})-close to pseudodifferential operators with symbols uu and π\pi both in Sρ0​(ε)S^{0}_{\rho}(\varepsilon).

We define the effective Hamiltonian h^\widehat{h} as the quantization of a resummation hh of the formal symbol

h=u​#​H​#​u∗.h=u\,\#\,H\,\#\,u^{*}\,. (23)

Recall that we do not distinguish semiclassical symbols and formal symbols in the notation. The following theorem is the basis for the adiabatic perturbation theory, as it relates the unitary time-evolution generated by the original Hamiltonian H^\widehat{H} to the one generated by the effective Hamiltonian h^\widehat{h}.

Theorem 4.1.

Under the assumptions of Theorem 3.1, one has that h∈Sρm​(ε)h\in S^{m}_{\rho}(\varepsilon) and h^\widehat{h} is essentially self-adjoint on 𝒮\mathcal{S}. Furthermore

[h^,Πr]=0,[\,\widehat{h},\,{\Pi_{\rm r}}\,]=0\,, (24)
e−i​H^​t−u^∗​e−i​h^​t​u^=𝒪0​(ε∞​|t|)e^{-i\widehat{H}t}-\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,e^{-i\widehat{h}t}\,\widehat{u}=\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}|t|) (25)

and

e−i​H^​t−U∗​e−i​h^​t​U=𝒪0​(ε∞​(1+|t|)).e^{-i\widehat{H}t}-U^{*}\,e^{-i\widehat{h}t}\,U=\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}(1+|t|))\,. (26)

Proof. Since u∈Sρ0​(ε)u\in S_{\rho}^{0}(\varepsilon) and H∈Sρm​(ε)H\in S_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon), the composition rule for semiclassical operators (see Prop. A.6) yields h∈Sρm​(ε)h\in S_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon) and thus hj∈Sρm−j​ρh_{j}\in S_{\rho}^{m-j\rho}.

Let h~:=u^​H^​u^∗\widetilde{h}:=\widehat{u}\,\widehat{H}\,\widehat{u}^{*}. Since u^∗\widehat{u}^{\,*} is bounded with bounded inverse, one finds, by checking definitions, that h~\widetilde{h} is self-adjoint on u^∗−1​D​(H^)\widehat{u}^{\,*\,-1}D(\widehat{H}) and that h~\widetilde{h} is essentially self-adjoint on u^∗−1​𝒮\widehat{u}^{\,*\,-1}\mathcal{S}. According to Equation (8.10) in [DiSj], which generalizes to ℬ⁡(ℋf)\mathcal{B(H}_{\rm f})-valued symbols, u^∗−1∈O​P​S0​(ε)\widehat{u}^{\,*\,-1}\in OPS^{0}(\varepsilon) and thus u^∗−1​𝒮=𝒮\widehat{u}^{\,*\,-1}\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}. Hence 𝒮\mathcal{S} is a core for h~\widetilde{h} and, since h^−h~∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)\widehat{h}-\widetilde{h}\in\mathcal{B(H)}, the same conclusions hold for h^\widehat{h}.

Next observe that, by construction, [hj,πr]=0[h_{j},\pi_{\mathrm{r}}]=0 for all j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N} and thus [hj,πr]#~=0[h_{j},\pi_{\mathrm{r}}]_{\widetilde{\#}}=0 because πr\pi_{\mathrm{r}} does not depend on (q,p)∈ℝ2​d(q,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}. Hence [h^j,Πr]=0[\widehat{h}_{j},{\Pi_{\rm r}}]=0 and thus (24) follows.

For (25) observe that

e−i​H^​t−u^∗e−i​h^​tu^=−ie−i​H^​t∫0tdsei​H^​s(H^u^∗−u^∗h^)e−i​h^​su^=𝒪0(ε∞|t|),e^{-i\widehat{H}t}-\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,e^{-i\widehat{h}t}\,\widehat{u}=-\,i\,e^{-i\widehat{H}t}\int_{0}^{t}\,ds\,e^{i\widehat{H}s}\left(\widehat{H}\,\widehat{u}^{\,*}-\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,\widehat{h}\right)e^{-i\widehat{h}s}\,\widehat{u}=\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}|t|)\,,

since, by construction, (H^​u^∗−u^∗​h^)=𝒪−∞​(ε∞)(\widehat{H}\,\widehat{u}^{\,*}-\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,\widehat{h})=\mathcal{O}_{-\infty}(\varepsilon^{\infty}). Finally (26) follows from (25) using U−u^=𝒪0​(ε∞)U-\widehat{u}=\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}). ∎

Remark 4.2.

It might seem more natural to define the effective Hamiltonian as

Heff=U​Π​H^​Π​U∗+U⁡(𝟏−Π)​H^​(𝟏−Π)​U∗.H_{\rm eff}=U\,\Pi\,\widehat{H}\,\Pi\,U^{*}+U\,({\bf 1}-\Pi)\,\widehat{H}\,({\bf 1}-\Pi)\,U^{*}\,.

Clearly one should have Heff−h^=𝒪⁡(ε∞)H_{\rm eff}-\widehat{h}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{\infty}) in some sense. However, if H^\widehat{H} is unbounded, this closeness does not follow in the norm of bounded operators from our results, since UU need not be a semiclassical operator. As a consequence no asymptotic expansion of HeffH_{\rm eff} in the norm of bounded operators would be available.

In the remainder of this section we will study the finite order asymptotic approximations

h^(n):=∑j=0nεj​h^j\widehat{h}^{(n)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\,\varepsilon^{j}\,\widehat{h}_{j}

to the effective Hamiltonian h^\widehat{h}. By virtue of (24), we can, whenever appropriate, restrict our attention to the reduced Hilbert space 𝒦=Ran​Πr\mathcal{K}=\mathrm{Ran}{\Pi_{\rm r}}. Furthermore we define u^(n)=∑j=0nεj​u^j\widehat{u}^{(n)}=\sum_{j=0}^{n}\,\varepsilon^{j}\,\widehat{u}_{j} and obtain a finite order expansion of the unitary UU as ‖U−u^(n)‖ℬ⁡(ℋ)=𝒪⁡(εn+1)\|\,U-\widehat{u}^{(n)}\,\|_{\mathcal{B(H)}}=\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{n+1}).

Our main interest are approximations to the solution of the time-dependent Schrödinger equation

i​∂ψt∂t=H^​ψti\,\frac{\partial\psi_{t}}{\partial t}=\widehat{H}\,\psi_{t}

over times of order ε−k​τ\varepsilon^{-k}\tau, where τ\tau does not depend on ε\varepsilon and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N} is arbitrary. Starting with (25) on the almost invariant subspace we obtain

e−i​H^​t​Π\displaystyle e^{-i\widehat{H}t}\Pi =\displaystyle= u^∗​e−i​h^​t​Πr​u^+𝒪0​(ε∞​|t|)\displaystyle\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,e^{-i\widehat{h}t}\,{\Pi_{\rm r}}\,\widehat{u}+\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}|t|) (27)
=\displaystyle= u^(n)∗e−i​t​h^(n+k)Πru^(n)+(1+|τ|)𝒪0(εn+1),|t|≤ε−kτ,\displaystyle\widehat{u}^{\,(n)*}\,e^{-it\widehat{h}^{(n+k)}}\,{\Pi_{\rm r}}\,\widehat{u}^{\,(n)}+(1+|\tau|)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{n+1})\,,\quad|t|\leq\varepsilon^{-k}\tau\,,

where ρ⁡(n+k+1)≥m\rho(n+k+1)\geq m is assumed in order to have h^−h^(n+k)∈ℬ⁡(ℋ)\widehat{h}-\widehat{h}^{(n+k)}\in\mathcal{B(H)}. Hence, given the level of precision εn\varepsilon^{n} and the time scale ε−k\varepsilon^{-k}, the expansion of h^\widehat{h} must be computed up to order h^n+k\widehat{h}_{n+k} and the expansion of UU up to order u^n\widehat{u}_{n}. Put differently, in order to improve the error, a better approximation to the unitary transformation is necessary. On the other hand, in order to enlarge the time-scale of validity for the space-adiabatic approximation, only the effective Hamiltonian h^\widehat{h} must be computed to higher orders.

Specializing (27) to n=0n=0 and k=1k=1, one obtains the leading order solution of the Schrödinger equation as

e−i​H^​t​Π=u^0∗​e−i⁡(h^0+ε​h^1)​t​Πr​u^0+(1+|τ|)​𝒪0​(ε),|t|≤ε−1​τ,e^{-i\widehat{H}t}\Pi=\widehat{u}_{0}^{*}\,e^{-i(\widehat{h}_{0}+\varepsilon\widehat{h}_{1})t}\,{\Pi_{\rm r}}\,\widehat{u}_{0}+(1+|\tau|)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon)\,,\quad|t|\leq\varepsilon^{-1}\tau\,, (28)

where m≤2​ρm\leq 2\rho. Here the choice of k=1k=1 corresponds to the macroscopic or semiclassical time-scale t/εt/\varepsilon. On this time-scale the effective dynamics e−ih^t/εΠre^{-i\widehat{h}t/\varepsilon}{\Pi_{\rm r}} on the reference subspace is expected to have a nice semiclassical limit, under suitable conditions on h^\widehat{h}.

Note that one can replace in (27) and analogously in (28) τ\tau by ε−δ​τ\varepsilon^{-\delta}\tau and obtains

e−i​H^​tΠ=u^(n)∗e−i​h^(n+k)Πru^(n)+(1+|τ|)𝒪0(εn+1−δ),|t|≤ε−(k+δ)τ.e^{-i\widehat{H}t}\Pi=\widehat{u}^{(n)*}\,e^{-i\widehat{h}^{(n+k)}}\,{\Pi_{\rm r}}\,\widehat{u}^{(n)}+(1+|\tau|)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{n+1-\delta})\,,\quad|t|\leq\varepsilon^{-(k+\delta)}\tau\,. (29)

Thus one can enlarge the time-span for which the approximation holds without the need to compute further terms in the expansion. The price to be paid is a larger error, of course.

We emphasize that (27) and (28) are purely space-adiabatic expansions with no semiclassical approximation invoked yet. As a consequence one obtains uniform results and a simple bound on the growth of the error with time. Note in particular that the space-adiabatic approximation holds on time-scales far beyond the Ehrenfest time-scale, the maximal time-scale for which semiclassical approximations are expected to hold. For some particular cases semiclassical expansions of the full propagator e−iH^t/εe^{-i\widehat{H}t/\varepsilon} have been derived directly, e.g. in the context of the Dirac equation [Ya, BoKe2]. These expansions hold, in general, only for short times, in the sense that they must be modified each time a caustic in the corresponding classical flow is encountered. More important, the clear separation of the space-adiabatic and the semiclassical expansion is not maintained, which is a severe drawback, since in many physical situations the space-adiabatic approximation is valid to high accuracy, while the semiclassical approximation is not, cf. Section 6. On the other hand, a semiclassical expansion of the right hand side of (28) is straightforward in many interesting cases, as will be discussed in Section 5.

In parentheses we remark that the space-adiabatic approximation can be used also in the time-independent setting, i.e. to estimate spectral properties of H^\widehat{H}. If one is able to compute eigenvalues of h^(n)\widehat{h}^{(n)} up to errors of order o⁡(εn)o(\varepsilon^{n}),

h^(n)​ψ(n)=E(n)​ψ(n)+o⁡(εn),\widehat{h}^{(n)}\,\psi^{(n)}=E^{(n)}\,\psi^{(n)}\,+\,o(\varepsilon^{n})\,,

it follows that

H^​u^∗​ψ(n)=E(n)​u^∗​ψ(n)+o⁡(εn).\widehat{H}\,\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,\psi^{(n)}=E^{(n)}\,\widehat{u}^{\,*}\,\psi^{(n)}\,+\,o(\varepsilon^{n})\,.

If, in addition, one knows from some a priori arguments that H^\widehat{H} has pure point spectrum near E(n)E^{(n)}, it follows that H^\widehat{H} has an eigenvalue o⁡(εn)o(\varepsilon^{n})-close to E(n)E^{(n)}. Otherwise one can at least conclude that there is a “resonance” in the sense of a quasi bound state o⁡(εn)o(\varepsilon^{n})-close to E(n)E^{(n)}. We stress that no explicit knowledge of UU is needed as long as the interest is in approximate eigenvalues only. For example, the scheme just described can be applied to the time-independent Born-Oppenheimer theory, where one is interested in the low lying spectrum of a molecule. The standard approaches to the time-independent Born-Oppenheimer approximation [CDS, Ha1, KMSW] yield in some respects mathematically stronger results. However, our scheme suffices for estimating asymptotic expansions of eigenvalues and is simpler to handle, in general.

4.2 Leading order terms in the expansion of the effective Hamiltonian

We turn to the explicit determination of the leading order terms hjh_{j} in the expansion of h^\widehat{h} using (23). Of course, in concrete applications only HH and u0u_{0} are given explicitly, while the higher order terms in the expansion of uu must be calculated using the construction from Section 3. For a general Hamiltonian H^\widehat{H} such a program is feasible only for the terms h0h_{0}, h1h_{1} and possibly h2h_{2}, which will be our concern in the following.

The principal symbol of hh is given by

h0=u0​H0​u0∗.h_{0}=u_{0}\,H_{0}\,u_{0}^{*}\,.

Higher order terms can be obtained using (23). The double Moyal product becomes rather awkward to handle, and alternatively we proceed inductively by observing that

u​#​H−h0​#​u=ε​h1​#​u+𝒪⁡(ε2)=ε​h1​u0+𝒪⁡(ε2),u\,\#\,H-h_{0}\,\#\,u=\varepsilon\,h_{1}\,\#\,u+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2})=\varepsilon\,h_{1}\,u_{0}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2})\,, (30)

with the subprincipal symbol on the left hand side being

(u​#​H−h0​#​u)1=u1​H0+u0​H1−h0​u1+(u0​#​H0)1−(h0​#​u0)1.\left(u\,\#\,H-h_{0}\,\#\,u\right)_{1}=u_{1}H_{0}+u_{0}H_{1}-h_{0}u_{1}+(u_{0}\,\#\,H_{0})_{1}-(h_{0}\,\#\,u_{0})_{1}\,. (31)

Recall the notation a​#​b=∑j=0∞εj​(a​#​b)ja\,\#\,b=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\,\varepsilon^{j}\,(a\,\#\,b)_{j} for the expansion of the Moyal product, see the Appendix. Combining (30) and (31) one obtains

h1=(u1​H0+u0​H1−h0​u1+(u0​#​H0)1−(h0​#​u0)1)​u0∗.h_{1}=\big(u_{1}H_{0}+u_{0}H_{1}-h_{0}u_{1}+(u_{0}\,\#\,H_{0})_{1}-(h_{0}\,\#\,u_{0})_{1}\,\big)\,u_{0}^{*}\,. (32)

The expression (32) further simplifies if one specializes to the case where σr​(q,p)={Er​(q,p)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\} consists of a single eigenvalue of H0​(q,p)H_{0}(q,p) and one projects on the relevant subspace,

πr​h1​πr=πr​(u0​H1​u0∗+(u0​#​H0)1​u0∗−(E∗​#​u0)1​u0∗)​πr.\pi_{\rm r}h_{1}\pi_{\rm r}=\pi_{\rm r}\big(u_{0}\,H_{1}\,u_{0}^{*}+(u_{0}\,\#\,H_{0})_{1}\,u_{0}^{*}-(E_{*}\,\#\,u_{0})_{1}\,u_{0}^{*}\big)\pi_{\rm r}\,. (33)

The right hand side has the nice property to be independent of u1u_{1} and thus to depend only on known quantities.

Along the same lines and under the same condition on σr​(q,p){\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p), one computes

πr​h2​πr\displaystyle\pi_{\rm r}h_{2}\pi_{\rm r} =\displaystyle= πr​(u0​H2+u1​H1−h1​u1CLOSE\displaystyle\pi_{\rm r}\Big(u_{0}H_{2}+u_{1}H_{1}-h_{1}u_{1} (34)
+(u1​#​H0)1+(u0​#​H1)1−(E∗​#​u1)1−(h1​#​u0)1\displaystyle+\,(u_{1}\,\#\,H_{0})_{1}+(u_{0}\,\#\,H_{1})_{1}-(E_{*}\,\#\,u_{1})_{1}-(h_{1}\,\#\,u_{0})_{1}
OPEN+(u0​#​H0)2−(E∗​#​u0)2)​u0∗​πr.\displaystyle+\,(u_{0}\,\#\,H_{0})_{2}-(E_{*}\,\#\,u_{0})_{2}\Big)u_{0}^{*}\pi_{\rm r}\,.

Again, (34) does not depend on u2u_{2} for the special case under consideration, but it does depend on u1u_{1}, which must now be computed using the construction from Section 3.

Although (34) looks still rather innocent, in general, it requires some work to compute it explicitly. This is partly because the second order expansion of the Moyal product in (34) tends to become rather tedious to obtain. But, in general, also the determination of u1u_{1} is nontrivial. To convince the reader, we state without details that the construction from Sections 2 and 3 yields

u1∗=u0∗​(−i4​{u0,u0∗}+[u0​π1OD​u0∗,πr]+i4​[({u0,π0}​u0∗+u0​{π0,u0∗}),πr]),u_{1}^{*}=u_{0}^{*}\Big(-\frac{i}{4}\{u_{0},u_{0}^{*}\}+\big[u_{0}\,\pi_{1}^{\rm OD}\,u_{0}^{*},\pi_{\rm r}\big]+\frac{i}{4}\big[\big(\{u_{0},\pi_{0}\}u_{0}^{*}+u_{0}\{\pi_{0},u_{0}^{*}\}\big),\pi_{\rm r}\big]\Big)\,, (35)

with

π1OD:=π0​π1​(1−π0)+(1−π0)​π1​π0,\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{OD}}:=\pi_{0}\pi_{1}(1-\pi_{0})+(1-\pi_{0})\pi_{1}\pi_{0}\,,

where we used that (a​#​b)1=−i2​{a,b}(a\,\#\,b)_{1}=-\frac{i}{2}\{a,b\}. Recall the definition (83) of the Poisson bracket {⋅,⋅}\{\cdot,\cdot\}.

To compute π1\pi_{1} from the given quantities one has to use the construction explained in Section 2. One finds

π1OD\displaystyle\pi_{1}^{\rm OD} =\displaystyle= i2​(R0​(E∗)​(1−π0)​{H0+E∗,π0}​π0CLOSE\displaystyle\frac{i}{2}\big(R_{0}(E_{*})(1-\pi_{0})\{H_{0}+E_{*},\pi_{0}\}\pi_{0}
OPEN+π0​{π0,H0+E∗}​R0​(E∗)​(1−π0))\displaystyle+\,\pi_{0}\,\{\pi_{0},H_{0}+E_{*}\}\,R_{0}(E_{*})\,(1-\pi_{0})\big)
+π0​H1​R0​(E∗)​(1−π0)+R0​(E∗)​(1−π0)​H1​π0,\displaystyle+\,\pi_{0}H_{1}R_{0}(E_{*})(1-\pi_{0})+R_{0}(E_{*})(1-\pi_{0})H_{1}\pi_{0}\,,

where R0​(Er)​(1−π0)=(H0−Er)−1​(1−π0)R_{0}({E_{\rm r}})(1-\pi_{0})=(H_{0}-{E_{\rm r}})^{-1}(1-\pi_{0}) is uniformly bounded because of the gap condition. For sake of completeness we mention that π1=π1OD+i2​{π0,π0}\pi_{1}=\pi_{1}^{\mathrm{OD}}+\frac{i}{2}\{\pi_{0},\pi_{0}\} in this case.

For the higher orders in the expansion of hh we only remark that, in general, hnh_{n} depends on u(n)u^{(n)}, H(n)H^{(n)} and h(n−1)h^{(n-1)}. In the special, but interesting case of an isolated eigenvalue Er​(q,p){E_{\rm r}}(q,p), hnh_{n} depends only on u(n−1)u^{(n-1)}, H(n)H^{(n)} and h(n−1)h^{(n-1)} and is thus considerably easier to obtain.

Remark 4.3.

Note that in the case of σr​(q,p)={Er​(q,p)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\}, not only the principal symbol h0​(q,p)=Er​(q,p)​𝟏ℋfh_{0}(q,p)={E_{\rm r}}(q,p){\bf 1}_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}}, but also the subprincipal symbol h1​(q,p)h_{1}(q,p) as given by (33) is well defined regardless of the gap condition, provided that the spectral projection π0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p) is sufficiently regular. Indeed, it can be shown, at least in some special cases, that there is still adiabatic decoupling to leading order and an effective dynamics generated by h^0+ε​h^1\widehat{h}_{0}+\varepsilon\,\widehat{h}_{1} without a gap condition [Te1], [Te2].

To get even more explicit formulas for h1h_{1} and h2h_{2}, note that in most applications one has no naturally given transformation u0u_{0}. Instead one chooses a suitable basis {ψα​(q,p)}α∈I\{\psi_{\alpha}(q,p)\}_{\alpha\in I} of Ranπ0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p) and defines u0​(q,p)=∑α∈I|χα⟩​⟨ψα​(q,p)|+r⁡(q,p)u_{0}(q,p)=\sum_{\alpha\in I}|\chi_{\alpha}\rangle\langle\psi_{\alpha}(q,p)|+r(q,p), where the vectors χα\chi_{\alpha} form a basis for Ranπr\pi_{\mathrm{r}} and r⁡(q,p)r(q,p) is some arbitrary unitary intertwining Ranπ0​(q,p)⟂\pi_{0}(q,p)^{\perp} and Ranπr⟂\pi_{\mathrm{r}}^{\perp}. πr​hj​(q,p)​πr\pi_{\mathrm{r}}\,h_{j}(q,p)\,\pi_{\mathrm{r}} is independent of the choice of the unitary r⁡(q,p)r(q,p) for all j∈ℕj\in\mathbb{N}.

We remark that such a basis {ψα​(q,p)}α∈I\{\psi_{\alpha}(q,p)\}_{\alpha\in I} of global smooth sections of the bundle over ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} defined by π0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p) always exists, since ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} is contractible (see Remark 3.5). However, we are not aware of a proof which insures u0∈Sρ0u_{0}\in S_{\rho}^{0} . The situation changes completely, once one considers local domains in the base space which are not contractible. Then it might become necessary to chose as reference space the space of sections of a globally nontrivial bundle.

Assuming that σr​(q,p)={Er​(q,p)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\} consists of a single eigenvalue of H0​(q,p)H_{0}(q,p) of multiplicity ℓ\ell (including ℓ=∞\ell=\infty), we obtain the ℓ×ℓ\ell\times\ell-matrix πr​h(1)​(q,p)​πr\pi_{\mathrm{r}}\,h^{(1)}(q,p)\,\pi_{\mathrm{r}} as

hα​β(1)=⟨χα,h(1)​χβ⟩=Er​δα​β+ε​h1​α​β,h_{\alpha\beta}^{(1)}=\langle\chi_{\alpha},h^{(1)}\chi_{\beta}\rangle={E_{\rm r}}\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}+\varepsilon\,h_{1\,\alpha\beta}\,, (36)

with

h1​α​β\displaystyle h_{1\,\alpha\beta} =\displaystyle= ⟨χα,h1​χβ⟩=⟨ψα,H1​ψβ⟩−i2​⟨ψα,{(H0+Er),ψβ}⟩\displaystyle\langle\chi_{\alpha},h_{1}\chi_{\beta}\rangle=\langle\psi_{\alpha},H_{1}\psi_{\beta}\rangle-\frac{i}{2}\langle\psi_{\alpha},\{(H_{0}+{E_{\rm r}}),\psi_{\beta}\}\rangle (37)
=\displaystyle= ⟨ψα,H1​ψβ⟩−i⁡⟨ψα,{Er,ψβ}⟩−i2​⟨ψα,{(H0−Er),ψβ}⟩.\displaystyle\langle\psi_{\alpha},H_{1}\psi_{\beta}\rangle-i\langle\psi_{\alpha},\{{E_{\rm r}},\psi_{\beta}\}\rangle-\frac{i}{2}\langle\psi_{\alpha},\{(H_{0}-{E_{\rm r}}),\psi_{\beta}\}\rangle\,.

The indices α\alpha and β\beta are matrix-indices, both running from 11 to ℓ\ell. Equations (36) and (37) are one of our central results. They are still of a simple form and mostly suffice to compute the basic physics. The first term in (36) is referred to as Peierls substitution and the first order correction carries information on the intraband spinor evolution. E.g., as will be discussed in Section 6, for the Dirac equation h1h_{1} governs the spin precession. The reason for the particular splitting of the terms in (37) will be discussed in Section 5. Here we only remark that the second term in (37) is related to a “generalized” Berry connection. We omit the analogous formula for h2​α​βh_{2\,\alpha\beta}, since it is too complicated to be helpful.

4.3 Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians

An instructive example to which formula (37) applies are Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians of the form

HBO​(q,p)=12​p2​𝟏ℋf+V⁡(q),H_{\mathrm{BO}}(q,p)=\frac{1}{2}p^{2}\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}}+V(q)\,, (38)

V∈S0​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))V\in S^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})), with an electronic energy band er​(q){e_{\rm r}}(q) of constant multiplicity ℓ\ell, i.e. V⁡(q)​π0​(q)=er​(q)​π0​(q)V(q)\pi_{0}(q)={e_{\rm r}}(q)\pi_{0}(q). Adiabatic decoupling for Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians is established with exponentially small errors by Martinez and Sordoni [MaSo], see also [So]. Their result partly triggered our interest to develop a general theory. Exponentially accurate coherent state solutions for Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians have been constructed by Hagedorn and Joye in [HaJo2].

Note that the quadratic growth of HBO​(q,p)H_{\mathrm{BO}}(q,p) as a function of pp prevents from applying the general results directly. As to be discussed in Section 4.5, energy cutoffs need to be introduced. For the moment we ignore this problem and proceed by working out the perturbative scheme formally.

We fix arbitrarily an orthonormal basis {ψα​(q)}α=1ℓ\{\psi_{\alpha}(q)\}_{\alpha=1}^{\ell} of Ranπ0​(q)\pi_{0}(q) depending smoothly on qq which then satisfies HBO​(q,p)​ψα​(q)=Er​(q,p)​ψα​(q)H_{\mathrm{BO}}(q,p)\psi_{\alpha}(q)={E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\psi_{\alpha}(q) with Er​(q,p)=12​p2+er​(q){E_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\frac{1}{2}p^{2}+{e_{\rm r}}(q) for 1≤α≤ℓ1\leq\alpha\leq\ell. Only the second term of our formula (37) contributes and yields

h1​α​β(q,p)=−ip⋅⟨ψα(q),∇qψβ(q)⟩=:−p⋅Aα​β(q),h_{1\,\alpha\beta}(q,p)=-i\,p\cdot\langle\psi_{\alpha}(q),\nabla_{q}\psi_{\beta}(q)\rangle=:-\,p\cdot A_{\alpha\beta}(q)\,,

which is well known in the case of a nondegenerate eigenvalue, [ShWi, LiWe, TeSp]. Aα​β​(q)A_{\alpha\beta}(q) has the geometrical meaning of a gauge potential, i.e. coefficients of a connection on the trivial bundle ℝd×ℂℓ\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{C}^{\ell}, the so called Berry connection. As mentioned already, a more detailed discussion of the origin of the Berry connection will be given in Section 5.

For the Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonian the calculation of h2​α​βh_{2\,\alpha\beta} is still feasible without much effort and the result is

h2​α​β\displaystyle h_{2\,\alpha\beta} =\displaystyle= 12​∑μ=1ℓAα​μ⋅Aμ​β+12​⟨∇qψα,(1−π0)⋅∇qψβ⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\mu=1}^{\ell}A_{\alpha\mu}\cdot A_{\mu\beta}+\frac{1}{2}\langle\nabla_{q}\psi_{\alpha},(1-\pi_{0})\cdot\nabla_{q}\psi_{\beta}\rangle (39)
−⟨p⋅∇qψα,R0​(Er)​p⋅∇qψβ⟩.\displaystyle-\,\langle\,p\cdot\nabla_{q}\psi_{\alpha},\,R_{0}({E_{\rm r}})\,\,p\cdot\nabla_{q}\psi_{\beta}\rangle\,.

Recall the definition of R0​(Er)=(H0−Er)−1​(1−π0)R_{0}({E_{\rm r}})=(H_{0}-{E_{\rm r}})^{-1}(1-\pi_{0}), which reduces to R0​(Er)​(q)=(V⁡(q)−er​(q))−1​(1−π0​(q))R_{0}({E_{\rm r}})(q)=(V(q)-{e_{\rm r}}(q))^{-1}(1-\pi_{0}(q)) in the present case. Although we omit the details of the computation leading to (39), we shortly describe how (34) relates to (39). Since H1=0H_{1}=0 and H2=0H_{2}=0 the corresponding terms in (34) do not contribute. Since u0u_{0} and π0\pi_{0} are functions of qq only, the second term in (35) is the only one contributing to u1u_{1}, and thus the third term in (34) also vanishes after projecting with the πr\pi_{\mathrm{r}}’s from outside the brackets. The last two terms in (34) cancel each other. The seventh term in (34) yields the first term in (39) and the fourth and sixth term in (34) combine to the second and third term in (39). In particular the calculation yields for the symbol of the unitary

uBO∗​(q,p)​πr=∑α=1ℓ(|ψα​(q)⟩+i​ε​R0​(Er)​(q)​|p⋅∇qψα​(q)⟩)​⟨χα|+𝒪⁡(ε2).u_{\mathrm{BO}}^{*}(q,p)\pi_{\mathrm{r}}=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{\ell}\Big(|\psi_{\alpha}(q)\rangle+i\varepsilon\,R_{0}({E_{\rm r}})(q)\,\,|\,p\cdot\nabla_{q}\psi_{\alpha}(q)\rangle\Big)\langle\chi_{\alpha}|+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2})\,.

Thus the symbol of the second order effective Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonian reads

hBO​α​β​(q,p)\displaystyle h_{\mathrm{BO}\,\alpha\beta}(q,p) =\displaystyle= 12​(p−ε​A​(q))α​β2+er​(q)​δα​β\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Big(p-\varepsilon\,A(q)\Big)^{2}_{\alpha\beta}+\,{e_{\rm r}}(q)\delta_{\alpha\beta} (40)
+ε22​⟨∇qψα​(q),(1−π0​(q))⋅∇qψβ​(q)⟩\displaystyle+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{2}\langle\nabla_{q}\psi_{\alpha}(q),(1-\pi_{0}(q))\cdot\nabla_{q}\psi_{\beta}(q)\rangle
−ε2​⟨p⋅∇qψα​(q),R0​(Er)​(q)​p⋅∇qψβ​(q)⟩+𝒪⁡(ε3),\displaystyle-\,\varepsilon^{2}\,\langle\,p\cdot\nabla_{q}\psi_{\alpha}(q),\,R_{0}({E_{\rm r}})(q)\,\,p\cdot\nabla_{q}\psi_{\beta}(q)\rangle+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{3})\,,

where the first term from (39) nicely completes the square to the first term in (40). Note that the third term on the right side of (40) depends on qq only and was interpreted in [ShWi] as a geometric electric potential in analogy to the geometric vector potential A⁡(q)A(q).

In the special case of a nondegenerate eigenvalue er{e_{\rm r}} and a matrix-valued Hamiltonian HH, (40) reduces to the expression obtained by Littlejohn and Weigert [LiWe]. They also remark that the previous studies [ShWi, AhSt] of the expansion of the effective Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonian missed the last term in (40). This strengthens our point of the usefulness of a general and systematic space-adiabatic perturbation theory.

The full power of our scheme is in force in cases where Ranπ0\pi_{0} is degenerate and depends both on qq and pp, since then the known techniques [LiFl, LiWe, NeSo, MaSo] cannot be applied. The simplest example of this kind is the one-particle Dirac equation with slowly varying electric and magnetic potentials, which will be discussed in Section 6.

4.4 The time-adiabatic theory revisited

With little additional effort our scheme can be applied even to the time-adiabatic setup. As for notation, we replace the phase space ℝqd×ℝpd\mathbb{R}^{d}_{q}\times\mathbb{R}^{d}_{p} by ℝt×ℝη\mathbb{R}_{t}\times\mathbb{R}_{\eta} in the following. Given a Hilbert space ℋ\mathcal{H} and family Hε​(t)H^{\varepsilon}(t), t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R} of self-adjoint operators such that Hε​(t)=:H⁡(t,η,ε)∈S0​(ε,ℬ⁡(ℋ))H^{\varepsilon}(t)=:H(t,\eta,\varepsilon)\in S^{0}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{B(H)}), the solutions of the equations

i​ε​∂tUε​(t,s)=Hε​(t)​Uε​(t,s),s∈ℝ,i\varepsilon\partial_{t}U^{\varepsilon}(t,s)=H^{\varepsilon}(t)U^{\varepsilon}(t,s)\,,\qquad s\in\mathbb{R}\,, (41)

define a unitary propagator. A unitary propagator is a unitary operator-valued map U⁡(t,s)U(t,s) strongly continuous in tt and ss jointly, such that

The following theorem is a variant of the time-adiabatic theorem of quantum mechanics [Ka2, ASY, JoPf, Ne1], however formulated in the language of adiabatic perturbation theory. Sjöstrand first recognized the usefulness of pseudodifferential calculus in this context [Sj] and we are grateful to G. Nenciu for pointing this out to us. We remark that the proof below can be adapted to the case of a time-dependent operator-valued classical symbol H⁡(q,p,t)H(q,p,t), as – for example – the Dirac Hamiltonian or the Pauli-Fierz Hamiltonian with slowly varying time-dependent external potentials.

4.5 Energy cutoff

The Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonians as well as many other physically relevant Hamiltonians do not satisfy the general assumptions we imposed in Sections 2 and 3. This is so for two reasons. First of all they are quantizations of symbols taking values in the unbounded operators. Secondly, the gap does not increase as fast as the Hamiltonian for large momenta, e.g. quadratically in the Born-Oppenheimer setting. The first problem is purely technical and the domain questions which arise have to be dealt with case by case. The second problem causes a qualitative change in the sense that the adiabatic decoupling is no longer uniform, as can be seen from the construction of the almost invariant subspace in Section 2. To deal with the second problem one therefore needs a cutoff for large momenta. There are basically two ways to implement such a cutoff. One possibility is to directly cut off large momenta as was done in [TeSp, SpTe], but then one needs to control the times for which no momenta exceeding the cutoff are produced under the dynamics. However, for a large class of Hamiltonians including the Born-Oppenheimer type Hamiltonian (38), cutting off high energies is equivalent to cutting high momenta. Then conservation of energy immediately ensures that no momenta exceeding the cutoff are produced over time. This idea was developped in [So] and also used in [MaSo]. We will briefly indicate an alternative way on how to implement such an energy cutoff in order to fit the Born-Oppenheimer and similar settings into our general assumptions.

Let H0∈S0mH_{0}\in S_{0}^{m} be elliptic and positive, i.e. there is a constant C>0C>0 such that H0​(q,p)≥C​⟨p⟩mH_{0}(q,p)\geq C\,\langle p\rangle^{m}. For example the Born-Oppenheimer Hamiltonian as defined in (38) satisfies H0∈S02H_{0}\in S^{2}_{0} and it is elliptic provided that VV is positive (otherwise just add a constant to H0H_{0} since V∈S0V\in S^{0}). Then we can prove adiabatic decoupling uniformly for energies below any λ∈ℝ\lambda\in\mathbb{R}, i.e. on Ran1​l(−∞,λ](H^0)\mathchoice{\hbox{${\rm 1}\hskip-2.3pt{\rm l}$}}{\hbox{${\rm 1}\hskip-2.3pt{\rm l}$}}{\hbox{$\scriptstyle{\rm I}\!{\rm N}$}}{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle{\rm I}\!{\rm N}$}}_{(-\infty,\lambda]}(\widehat{H}_{0}).

Let Λ={(q,p):H0​(q,p)<λ}\Lambda=\{(q,p):H_{0}(q,p)<\lambda\}, then bounding the total energy by λ\lambda essentially corresponds to confining the slow degrees of freedom to the region Λ\Lambda in phase space. More precisely, let χλ∈C0∞​(ℝ)\chi_{\lambda}\in C_{0}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) such that χλ|[0,λ]=1\chi_{\lambda}|_{[0,\lambda]}=1 and χλ|[λ+δ,∞)=0\chi_{\lambda}|_{[\lambda+\delta,\infty)}=0 for some δ>0\delta>0, then χλ​(H^0)∈OP​S0−∞\chi_{\lambda}(\widehat{H}_{0})\in\mathrm{OP}S^{-\infty}_{0} is a semiclassical operator. 5 Semiclassical analysis for effective Hamiltonians

The results of the previous sections are genuine quantum mechanical: semiclassical symbols have been used only as a tool in order to construct (and, eventually, to approximate) Π\Pi and UU, but no semiclassical limit has been performed. Indeed, the adiabatic decoupling of energy bands is a purely quantum phenomenon, which is, in general, independent from the semiclassical limit.

However, under the assumption that σr​(q,p)={Er​(q,p)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\} consists of a single eigenvalue of H0​(q,p)H_{0}(q,p) of necessarily constant multiplicity ℓ\ell, the principal symbol of h^\widehat{h} is a scalar multiple of the identity, i.e. h0​(q,p)​πr=Er​(q,p)​𝟏𝒦fh_{0}(q,p)\pi_{\mathrm{r}}={E_{\rm r}}(q,p){\bf 1}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}}, and a semiclassical analysis of h^\widehat{h} can be done in a standard way. In particular, the dynamics of quantum observables can be approximated by quantities constructed using only the classical flow Φt\Phi^{t} generated by the (classical, scalar) Hamiltonian Er​(q,p){E_{\rm r}}(q,p). This results in a generalized Egorov’s theorem, see Theorem 5.1. We emphasize that for more general energy bands σr​(q,p){\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p) one cannot expect a simple semiclassical limit, at least not in the usual sense.

5.1 Semiclassical analysis for matrix-valued symbols

+i⁡[h2,a0​(t)]\displaystyle+\,i[h_{2},a_{0}(t)]

Since d​an​(t)/d​tda_{n}(t)/dt does not depend on higher orders, the equations can be solved iteratively. The solution of (51) with initial condition a0​(q,p,0)=a0​(q,p)a_{0}(q,p,0)=a_{0}(q,p) is given through

a0​(q,p,t)=D∗​(q,p,t)​a0​(Φt​(q,p))​D​(q,p,t),a_{0}(q,p,t)=D^{*}(q,p,t)\,a_{0}(\Phi^{t}(q,p))\,D(q,p,t)\,, (54)

where Φt:ℝ2​d→ℝ2​d\Phi^{t}:\mathbb{R}^{2d}\to\mathbb{R}^{2d} is the solution flow corresponding to the scalar Hamiltonian Er​(q,p){E_{\rm r}}(q,p). More precisely, Φt​(q0,p0)=(q⁡(t),p⁡(t))\Phi^{t}(q_{0},p_{0})=(q(t),p(t)), where (q⁡(t),p⁡(t))(q(t),p(t)) is the solution of the classical equations of motion

with initial condition (q0,p0)(q_{0},p_{0}). D⁡(q,p,t)D(q,p,t) is the solution of

∂∂t​D​(q,p,t)=−i​h1​(Φt​(q,p))​D​(q,p,t).\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\,D(q,p,t)=-\,i\,h_{1}(\Phi^{t}(q,p))\,D(q,p,t)\,. (55)

with initial condition D⁡(q,p,0)=𝟏D(q,p,0)=\mathbf{1}. Since h1​(q,p)h_{1}(q,p) is self-adjoint for all (q,p)∈ℝ2​d(q,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}, the solution D⁡(q,p,t)D(q,p,t) of (55) is unitary for all (q,p,t)∈ℝ2​d×ℝ(q,p,t)\in\mathbb{R}^{2d}\times\mathbb{R}.

To see that (54) is indeed the solution of (51), note that the mappings

defined through (54) for t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, i.e.

form a one-parameter group of linear automorphisms on the Banach space Cb​(ℝ2​dCLOSE,C_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathbb{R}^{2d}, OPENℬ⁡(ℂℓ))\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}^{\ell})), since

(𝒰⁡(s)​𝒰​(t)​a0)​(q,p)=\displaystyle\hskip-14.22636pt\big(\mathcal{U}(s)\,\mathcal{U}(t)\,a_{0}\big)(q,p)=
=\displaystyle= D∗​(q,p,s)​D∗​(Φs​(q,p),t)​a0​(Φs∘Φt​(q,p))​D​(Φs​(q,p),t)​D​(q,p,s)\displaystyle D^{*}(q,p,s)\,D^{*}(\Phi^{s}(q,p),t)\,a_{0}(\Phi^{s}\circ\Phi^{t}(q,p))\,D(\Phi^{s}(q,p),t)\,D(q,p,s)
=\displaystyle= D∗​(q,p,t+s)​a0​(Φt+s​(q,p))​D​(q,p,t+s)\displaystyle D^{*}(q,p,t+s)\,a_{0}(\Phi^{t+s}(q,p))\,D(q,p,t+s)
=\displaystyle= (𝒰⁡(t+s)​a0)​(q,p).\displaystyle\big(\mathcal{U}(t+s)a_{0}\big)(q,p)\,.

Here the group structures of Φt\Phi^{t} and of the solutions of (55) are used. Hence 𝒰⁡(t)\mathcal{U}(t) is a group and it suffices to check that (54) solves (51) at time t=0t=0, which is easy to see.

The physical interpretation becomes simpler when translated to states: a “classical” particle which started at time 00 at the phase space point (q,p)(q,p) with spinor φ0∈ℂℓ\varphi_{0}\in\mathbb{C}^{\ell}, is at time tt located at the phase space point Φt​(q,p)\Phi^{t}(q,p) with spinor φt=D⁡(q,p,t)​φ0\varphi_{t}=D(q,p,t)\varphi_{0}. Hence (55) implies that

d​φtd​t=−i​h1​(Φt​(q,p))​φt.\frac{d\varphi_{t}}{dt}=-\,i\,h_{1}(\Phi^{t}(q,p))\,\varphi_{t}\,. (57)

One can also think of 𝒰⁡(t)\mathcal{U}(t) as being the action on observables of a “classical” flow Φℓt\Phi_{\ell}^{t} on phase space ℝ2​d×SU​(ℓ)\mathbb{R}^{2d}\times\mbox{SU}(\ell) defined as

Φℓt​(q,p,U)=(Φt​(q,p),D⁡(q,p,t)​U).\Phi_{\ell}^{t}(q,p,U)=(\Phi^{t}(q,p),D(q,p,t)\,U)\,.

Turning to the higher order corrections (52), (53) etc., they are of the form

d​an​(t)d​t={Er​𝟏,an​(t)}+i⁡[h1,an​(t)]+In​(a0​(t),…,an−1​(t))\frac{d\,a_{n}(t)}{dt}=\{{E_{\rm r}}\mathbf{1},a_{n}(t)\}+i[h_{1},a_{n}(t)]+I_{n}(a_{0}(t),\ldots,a_{n-1}(t))

with an inhomogeneity In​(t)I_{n}(t) depending only on the known functions a0​(t),a_{0}(t), …,an−1​(t)\ldots,a_{n-1}(t). Thus, assuming an​(0)=0a_{n}(0)=0, one finds

an​(t)=∫0td​s​𝒰​(t−s)​In​(s).a_{n}(t)=\int_{0}^{t}\,ds\,\mathcal{U}(t-s)\,I_{n}(s)\,. (58)

In order to solve Equation (52) for the subprincipal symbol one needs to know h2h_{2}. However, if one is interested in semiclassical observables with a principal symbol which is a scalar multiple of the identity, e.g. in the position a0​(0)=q​ 1a_{0}(0)=q\,\mathbf{1}, the last term in ( 52) vanishes at all times, since, according to (54), a0​(t)a_{0}(t) is a scalar multiple of the identity for all times. In Section 6 the back reaction of the spin of an electron on its translational motion will be discussed on the basis of (52).

We summarize the preceding discussion on Egorov’s theorem.

Theorem 5.1 (Egorov).

Let HH satisfy either (IG)m for m≤1m\leq 1 and ρ=1\rho=1 or (CG) with ρ=0\rho=0. Let σr​(q,p)={Er​(q,p)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\} be an eigenvalue of H0​(q,p)H_{0}(q,p) of finite multiplicity ℓ\ell.

Then the classical flow Φt\Phi^{t} generated by Er​(q,p){E_{\rm r}}(q,p) and the solution of (55) with initial condition D⁡(q,p,0)=𝟏D(q,p,0)=\mathbf{1} exist globally in time. For a0∈Sρ0​(ℬ⁡(ℂℓ))a_{0}\in S_{\rho}^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}^{\ell})), a0​(t)a_{0}(t) given by (54) is a solution of (51) and a0​(t)∈Sρ0​(ℬ⁡(ℂℓ))a_{0}(t)\in S_{\rho}^{0}(\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{C}^{\ell})) for all tt.

For each T<∞T<\infty there is a constant CT<∞C_{T}<\infty such that for all t∈[−T,T]t\in[-T,T]

‖a⁡(t)−𝒲ε​(a0​(t))‖≤ε​CT,\left\|a(t)\,-\,\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}\left(a_{0}(t)\right)\right\|\,\leq\,\varepsilon\,C_{T}\,, (59)
