Proof. Up to the modifications discussed before, the proof follows easily along the lines of Egorov’s theorem for scalar valued observables (cf. [Ro, BoRo]): To make the expansion of the Heisenberg equation (50) rigorous, note that Er=πr​h0​πr∈Sρm​(ℝ){E_{\rm r}}=\pi_{\mathrm{r}}h_{0}\pi_{\mathrm{r}}\in S_{\rho}^{m}(\mathbb{R}) with m≤1m\leq 1 and thus the corresponding Hamiltonian vector field is smooth and bounded. It follows by standard ODE techniques [Ro] that ∂ta0​(Φt)∈S10\partial_{t}a_{0}(\Phi^{t})\in S^{0}_{1} and hence also ∂ta0​(t)∈S10\partial_{t}a_{0}(t)\in S^{0}_{1}, where a0​(t)a_{0}(t) is given by (54). Thus one can interchange quantization and differentiation with respect to time and obtains

a(t)−𝒲ε(a0(t))=∫0tdsdd​s(ei​h^​s/ε𝒲ε(a0(t−s))e−ih^s/ε)\displaystyle a(t)-\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}(a_{0}(t))=\int_{0}^{t}\,ds\,\frac{d}{ds}\left(e^{i\widehat{h}s/\varepsilon}\,\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}(a_{0}(t-s))\,e^{-i\widehat{h}s/\varepsilon}\right)
=\displaystyle= ∫0tdsei​h^​s/ε(iε[h^,𝒲ε(a0(t−s))]−𝒲ε(d​a0d​t(t−s)))e−ih^s/ε.\displaystyle\int_{0}^{t}\,ds\,e^{i\widehat{h}s/\varepsilon}\,\left(\frac{i}{\varepsilon}\left[\,\widehat{h},\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}(a_{0}(t-s))\,\right]-\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{da_{0}}{dt}(t-s)\right)\right)e^{-i\widehat{h}s/\varepsilon}\,.

Now, by construction, iε​[h^,a0​(t−s)^]−𝒲ε​(d​a0d​t​(t−s))\frac{i}{\varepsilon}\left[\widehat{h},\widehat{a_{0}(t-s)}\right]-\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}\left(\frac{da_{0}}{dt}(t-s)\right) is a semiclassical operator in OPS11​(ε)S_{1}^{1}(\varepsilon) with vanishing principal symbol. Hence the integrand is really 𝒪⁡(ε)\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) as a bounded operator and (59) follows. ∎

This matrix-valued version of Egorov’s theorem has been discussed several times in the literature [Iv, BrNo].

Berry connection. With this preparation we explain the motivation behind the particular splitting of the terms in (37). It is of geometrical origin and related to the Berry connection. Recall that in the Born-Oppenheimer setting h1​α​β(q,p)=−p⋅Aα​β(q)h_{1\,\alpha\beta}(q,p)=-p\cdot A_{\alpha\beta}(q) and thus Aα​β​(q)A_{\alpha\beta}(q) acts as a gauge potential of a connection on the trivial bundle ℝd×ℂℓ\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{C}^{\ell}. Its origin is purely geometrical, since it comes from the connection which the trivial connection on the trivial bundle ℝd×ℋf\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}} induces on the subbundle defined by π0​(q)\pi_{0}(q). If one assumes that Ranπ0​(q)\pi_{0}(q) is 11-dimensional, the internal rotations along classical trajectories are just phase changes, the so called Berry phases, and are due to parallel transport with respect to the Berry connection [Be, ShWi, Si].

In the general case the second term of h1​α​β​(q,p)h_{1\,\alpha\beta}(q,p) in (37), which we denote by

hBe​α​β​(q,p)=−i⁡⟨ψα​(q,p),{Er,ψβ}​(q,p)⟩,h_{\mathrm{Be\,\alpha\beta}}(q,p)=-i\langle\psi_{\alpha}(q,p),\{{E_{\rm r}},\psi_{\beta}\}(q,p)\rangle,

corresponds exactly to this parallel transport along the generalized Berry connection. More precisely, the trivial connection on the trivial bundle ℝ2​d×ℋf\mathbb{R}^{2d}\times\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}} induces a U⁡(ℓ)U(\ell)-connection on the subbundle defined by π0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p). After unitary rotation u0​(q,p)u_{0}(q,p) the coefficients of this connection on the bundle ℝ2​d×ℂℓ\mathbb{R}^{2d}\times\mathbb{C}^{\ell} are

Aα​β​(q,p)=i​(⟨ψα​(q,p),∇qψβ​(q,p)⟩⟨ψα​(q,p),∇pψβ​(q,p)⟩),A_{\alpha\beta}(q,p)=\,i\,\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\langle\psi_{\alpha}(q,p),\nabla_{q}\psi_{\beta}(q,p)\rangle\\ \langle\psi_{\alpha}(q,p),\nabla_{p}\psi_{\beta}(q,p)\rangle\end{array}\right)\,,

in the sense that a section s⁡(q,p)s(q,p) is parallel if (∇−i​A)​s=0(\nabla-iA)s=0. It is parallel along some curve c⁡(τ)=(q⁡(τ),p⁡(τ))c(\tau)=\big(q(\tau),p(\tau)\big) in ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d} if

(∂τ−c˙(τ)⋅iA(q(τ),p(τ)))s(q(τ),p(τ))=0.\Big(\partial_{\tau}-\dot{c}(\tau)\cdot iA\big(q(\tau),p(\tau)\big)\Big)s\big(q(\tau),p(\tau)\big)=0\,.

For classical trajectories, where c˙​(t)=(∇pEr,−∇qEr)T\dot{c}(t)=(\nabla_{p}{E_{\rm r}},-\nabla_{q}{E_{\rm r}})^{\mathrm{T}}, this condition becomes

(∂t+ihBe(q(t),p(t)))s(q(t),p(t))=0.\Big(\partial_{t}+i\,h_{\mathrm{Be}}\big(q(t),p(t)\big)\Big)s\big(q(t),p(t)\big)=0\,. (60)

If h1=hBeh_{1}=h_{\mathrm{Be}}, (60) is exactly Equation (57) for the rotation of the spinor φt​(q⁡(t),p⁡(t))=D⁡(q,p,t)​φ0\varphi_{t}\big(q(t),p(t)\big)=D\big(q,p,t\big)\varphi_{0} along the trajectory of the particle. This means if h1=hBeh_{1}=h_{\mathrm{Be}}, the spin dynamics corresponds to parallel transport with respect to the Berry connection along classical trajectories.

Emmrich and Weinstein [EmWe] give a geometric meaning also to the remaining terms in their analog of h1h_{1}. While this is a natural venture in the context of geometric WKB approximation, it seems to be less natural in our approach, since we work in a fixed basis in order to obtain simple analytic expressions.

Wigner function approach. The previous results on the time-evolution of semiclassical observables translate, by the duality expressed through

⟨ψ,a^0​ψ⟩=∫ℝ2​dTrℂℓ​(a0​(q,p)​Wψ​(q,p))​𝑑q​𝑑p,\langle\psi,\,\widehat{a}_{0}\,\psi\rangle=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\,{\rm Tr}_{\mathbb{C}^{\ell}}\left(a_{0}(q,p)W^{\psi}(q,p)\right)\,dq\,dp\,,

to the time-evolution of the Wigner transform

Wψ​(q,p):=Symb⁡(Pψ)​(q,p)=(2​π)−d​∫ℝdd​ξ​ei​ξ⋅p​ψ​(q+ε​ξ/2)⊗ψ∗​(q−ε​ξ/2)W^{\psi}(q,p):={\rm Symb}(P_{\psi})(q,p)=(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\,d\xi\,e^{i\xi\cdot p}\,\psi(q+\varepsilon\xi/2)\otimes\psi^{*}(q-\varepsilon\xi/2)

as

⟨ψ,a^0​(t)​ψ⟩=\displaystyle\langle\psi,\,\widehat{a}_{0}(t)\,\psi\rangle=
=∫ℝ2​dTrℂℓ​(a0​(q,p)​D∗​(q,p,−t)​Wψ​(Φ−t​(q,p))​D​(q,p,−t))​𝑑q​𝑑p+𝒪⁡(ε).\displaystyle\hskip-13.0pt=\,\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\hskip-2.0pt{\rm Tr}_{\mathbb{C}^{\ell}}\left(a_{0}(q,p)\,D^{*}(q,p,-t)\,W^{\psi}(\Phi^{-t}(q,p))\,D(q,p,-t)\right)\,dq\,dp+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)\,.

Transport equations for matrix-valued Wigner measures were derived in [GMMP] and applied to the Dirac equation in [Sp].

Semiclassical propagator. Often one is not only interested in the semiclassical propagation of observables, but more directly in a semiclassical expansion of the kernel K⁡(x,y,t)K(x,y,t) of the unitary group

(e−ih^t/εψ)(x)=∫ℝddyKε(x,y,t)ψ(y).\big(e^{-i\widehat{h}t/\varepsilon}\psi\big)(x)=\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\,dy\,K^{\varepsilon}(x,y,t)\,\psi(y)\,. (61)

As in the case of Egorov’s theorem, generalizing the known results for Hamiltonians with scalar symbols to the case of operator-valued symbols is straightforward, whenever the principal symbol h0h_{0} of hh is a scalar multiple of the identity. As in the scalar case, see [Ro], one makes an ansatz of the form

Kε​(x,y,t)=1(2​π​ε)d​∫ℝdd​p​eiε​(S​(x,p,t)−y⋅p)​(∑j=0∞εj​aj​(x,p,t)),K^{\varepsilon}(x,y,t)=\frac{1}{(2\pi\varepsilon)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{d}}\,dp\,e^{\frac{i}{\varepsilon}\big(S(x,p,t)-y\cdot p\big)}\Big(\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}\varepsilon^{j}a_{j}(x,p,t)\Big)\,,

where S⁡(x,p,t)S(x,p,t) is real valued and the aja_{j}’s take values in the bounded linear operators on ℂℓ\mathbb{C}^{\ell}. Demanding (61) at time t=0t=0, i.e. Kε​(x,y,0)=δ⁡(x−y)K^{\varepsilon}(x,y,0)=\delta(x-y), imposes the following initial conditions on SS and {aj}j≥0\{a_{j}\}_{j\geq 0}:

S(x,p,0)=x⋅p,a0(x,p,0)=𝟏andaj(x,p,0)=0forj≥1.S(x,p,0)=x\cdot p\,,\qquad a_{0}(x,p,0)=\mathbf{1}\quad\mbox{and}\quad a_{j}(x,p,0)=0\quad\mbox{for}\,j\geq 1\,.

For later times the coefficients are determined by formally expanding the Schrödinger equation for Kε​(x,y,t)K^{\varepsilon}(x,y,t)

i​ε​∂∂t​Kε​(⋅,y,t)=h^​Kε​(⋅,y,t)i\,\varepsilon\frac{\partial}{\partial t}K^{\varepsilon}(\cdot,y,t)=\widehat{h}\,K^{\varepsilon}(\cdot,y,t)

in orders of ε\varepsilon. At leading order only h^0=E^0\widehat{h}_{0}=\widehat{E}_{0} contributes and one obtains as in the scalar case

∂tS⁡(x,p,t)+Er​(x,∇xS​(x,p,t))=0,\partial_{t}\,S(x,p,t)+{E_{\rm r}}\big(x,\nabla_{x}S(x,p,t)\big)=0\,, (62)

the Hamilton-Jacobi equation for the symbol h0h_{0}. The next to leading order equation is the so called transport equation for a0a_{0}:

i​∂ta0​(x,p,t)=ℒ⁡(x,p,t)​a0​(x,p,t)+h1​(x,∇xS​(x,p,t))​a0​(x,p,t).i\partial_{t}a_{0}(x,p,t)=\mathcal{L}(x,p,t)\,a_{0}(x,p,t)\,+h_{1}\big(x,\nabla_{x}S(x,p,t)\big)\,a_{0}(x,p,t)\,. (63)

The differential operator ℒ⁡(x,p,t)\mathcal{L}(x,p,t) is the same as in the scalar case, see [Ro] for an explicit formula. Here we just want to point out that the known techniques from the scalar case apply with one modification: as in (51), also in (63) h1h_{1} contributes as an additional rotation in the transport equation for the leading order term. Since the solution of (62) exists only until a caustic is reached, the approximation (62), (63) to the propagator is a short time result only. The extension to arbitrary times is a complicated task, in general [MaFe].

5.2 An Egorov theorem

Ultimately the goal is to approximate expectation values of observables in in the original Hilbert space ℋ=L2​(ℝd,ℋf)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}) rather than in ℋ=L2​(ℝd,𝒦f)\mathcal{H}=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}). Before stating a theorem an obvious, but important observation should be made, which seems to have been overlooked, or at least not stressed sufficiently, in related discussions, e.g., [LiFl, LiWe, BoKe2, MaSo]: We proved that in the case σr​(q,p)={Er​(q,p)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\} the effective Hamiltonian h^\widehat{h} projected on the subspace 𝒦=Ran​Πr\mathcal{K}=\mbox{Ran}{\Pi_{\rm r}} has a semiclassical limit in the sense of a generalized Egorov theorem, in principle, to any order in ε\varepsilon. However, the variables qq and pp in the rotated representation are not the canonical variables of the slow degrees of freedom in the original problem. More precisely, let q^ℋ=x⊗𝟏ℋf\widehat{q}_{\mathcal{H}}=x\otimes\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}} and p^ℋ=−iε∇x⊗𝟏ℋf\widehat{p}_{\mathcal{H}}=-i\varepsilon\nabla_{x}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}} be the position and momentum operators of the slow degrees of freedom acting on ℋ\mathcal{H} and let q^𝒦=x⊗𝟏𝒦f\widehat{q}_{\mathcal{K}}=x\otimes\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}} and p^𝒦=−iε∇x⊗𝟏𝒦f\widehat{p}_{\mathcal{K}}=-i\varepsilon\nabla_{x}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{K}_{\mathrm{f}}} be the same operators acting on 𝒦\mathcal{K}. Then q^𝒦=Πr​U​q^ℋ​U∗​Πr+𝒪⁡(ε)\widehat{q}_{\mathcal{K}}={\Pi_{\rm r}}U\,\widehat{q}_{\mathcal{H}}\,U^{*}\,{\Pi}_{\mathrm{r}}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) and p^𝒦=Πr​U​p^ℋ​U∗​Πr+𝒪⁡(ε)\widehat{p}_{\mathcal{K}}={\Pi_{\rm r}}\,U\,\widehat{p}_{\mathcal{H}}\,U^{*}\,{\Pi}_{\mathrm{r}}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon), with a, in general, nonvanishing ε\varepsilon-correction. Physically this means that the quantities which behave like position and momentum in the semiclassical limit are only close to the position and momentum of the slow degrees of freedom, but not equal. This phenomenon is well known in the case of the nonrelativistic limit of the Dirac equation. The Newton-Wigner position operator and not the standard position operator goes over to the position operator in the Pauli equation. The standard position operator has neither a nice nonrelativistic limit nor, as we will see, a nice semiclassical limit, because of the Zitterbewegung. Switching to the Newton-Wigner position operator corresponds to averaging over the Zitterbewegung, or, in our language, to use the position operator q^𝒦\widehat{q}_{\mathcal{K}} in the rotated representation. We remark that in the Born-Oppenheimer case, and more generally whenever π0\pi_{0} depends on qq only, one has q^𝒦=Πr​U​q^ℋ​U∗​Πr+𝒪⁡(ε2)\widehat{q}_{\mathcal{K}}={\Pi_{\rm r}}U\,\widehat{q}_{\mathcal{H}}\,U^{*}\,{\Pi_{\rm r}}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{2}).

With this warning we exploit that semiclassical observables do not change after unitary rotation in leading order and state the Egorov theorem for the observables in the original representation.

Corollary 5.2.

Let HH satisfy either (IG)m with m≤1m\leq 1 and ρ=1\rho=1 or (CG) with ρ=0\rho=0 and let σr​(q,p)={Er​(q,p)}{\sigma_{\rm r}}(q,p)=\{{E_{\rm r}}(q,p)\} consist of a single eigenvalue of H0​(q,p)H_{0}(q,p) of finite multiplicity ℓ\ell. Let b0∈S10​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))b_{0}\in S_{1}^{0}(\mathcal{B(H}_{\mathrm{f}})) such that [b0,π0]=0[b_{0},\pi_{0}]=0 and B(t):=ei​H^​t/εb^0e−iH^t/εB(t):=e^{i\widehat{H}t/\varepsilon}\,\widehat{b}_{0}\,e^{-i\widehat{H}t/\varepsilon}. Let a0:=πr​u0​b0​u0∗​πra_{0}:=\pi_{\mathrm{r}}\,u_{0}\,b_{0}\,u_{0}^{*}\,\pi_{\mathrm{r}} and define a0​(t)a_{0}(t) is in (54). Then for each T<∞T<\infty there is a constant CT<∞C_{T}<\infty such that for all t∈[−T,T]t\in[-T,T]

‖(B⁡(t)−𝒲ε​(u0∗​a0​(t)​u0))​Π‖≤ε​CT.\left\|\big(B(t)\,-\,\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}(u_{0}^{*}\,a_{0}(t)\,u_{0})\big)\Pi\right\|\,\leq\,\varepsilon\,C_{T}\,. (64)

For b0=f​ 1ℋfb_{0}=f\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}}, with f∈S10​(ℝ)f\in S_{1}^{0}(\mathbb{R}), one obtains as a special case of (64) that

‖(B⁡(t)−b0​(Φt)^)​Π‖≤ε​CT.\left\|\big(B(t)\,-\,\widehat{b_{0}(\Phi^{t})}\big)\Pi\right\|\,\leq\,\varepsilon\,C_{T}\,.

Corollary 5.2 follows from Theorem 5.1 and a straightforward expansion in ε\varepsilon of the terms to be estimated after rotation with UU.

6 The Dirac equation

6.1 Adiabatic decoupling of electrons and positrons

We apply the adiabatic perturbation theory to the one-particle Dirac equation with slowly varying external potentials, i.e. to

H~D=c​α⋅(−i​ℏ​∇y−ec​A​(ε​y))+β​m​c2+e​ϕ​(ε​y)\widetilde{H}_{\mathrm{D}}=c\alpha\cdot\left(-i\hbar\nabla_{y}-\frac{e}{c}A(\varepsilon y)\right)+\beta mc^{2}+e{\phi}(\varepsilon y)\,

acting on L2​(ℝ3,ℂ4)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{4}). Here A:ℝ3→ℝ3A:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R}^{3} is the vector potential of an external magnetic field B=∇∧AB=\nabla\wedge A and ϕ:ℝ3→ℝ{\phi}:\mathbb{R}^{3}\to\mathbb{R} the potential of an external electric field E=−∇ϕE=-\nabla{\phi}. For the Dirac matrices α\alpha, β\beta we make the standard choice

α=(0σσ0),β=(𝟏ℂ200−𝟏ℂ2),\alpha=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&\sigma\\ \sigma&0\end{array}\right)\,,\qquad\beta=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}&0\\ 0&-\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}\end{array}\right)\,,

where σ=(σ1,σ2,σ3)\sigma=(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\sigma_{3}) denotes the vector of the Pauli spin matrices. The small parameter ε>0\varepsilon>0 controls the variation of the external potentials. To keep track of the size of the error terms, in this section all physical constants, including ℏ\hbar, are displayed.

Transforming to the macroscopic space-scale x=ε​yx=\varepsilon y one obtains the Dirac Hamiltonian

H^D=c​α⋅(−i​ε​ℏ​∇x−ec​A​(x))+β​m​c2+e​ϕ​(x)\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}}=c\alpha\cdot\left(-i\varepsilon\hbar\nabla_{x}-\frac{e}{c}A(x)\right)+\beta mc^{2}+e{\phi}(x)\, (65)

and we are interested in the solution of the time-dependent Dirac equation for times of order ε−1\varepsilon^{-1}, i.e. in solutions of

i​ε​ℏ​∂∂t​ψt=H^D​ψti\,\varepsilon\hbar\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\psi_{t}=\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}}\,\psi_{t} (66)

for |t|=𝒪⁡(1)|t|=\mathcal{O}(1). The solutions of (66) for small ε\varepsilon approximately describe the dynamics of electrons, resp. positrons, in weak fields, as in storage rings, accelerators, or cloud chambers, for example.

H^D\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}} is the Weyl quantization of the matrix-valued function

HD​(q,p)=c​α⋅(p−ec​A​(q))+β​m​c2+e​ϕ​(q)H_{\mathrm{D}}(q,p)=c\alpha\cdot\left(p-\frac{e}{c}A(q)\right)+\beta mc^{2}+e{\phi}(q)

on phase space ℝ6\mathbb{R}^{6}, where now Weyl quantization is in the sense of p↦−i​ε​ℏ​∇xp\mapsto-i\varepsilon\hbar\nabla_{x}, i.e. on the right hand side of (78) ε\varepsilon must be replaced by ε​ℏ\varepsilon\hbar. ℏ\hbar appears here for dimensional reasons and is a fixed physical constant. The small parameter of the space-adiabatic expansion is ε\varepsilon. HD​(q,p)H_{\mathrm{D}}(q,p) has two two-fold degenerate eigenvalues

E±​(q,p)=±c​p0​(q,p)+e​ϕ​(q)E_{\pm}(q,p)=\pm cp_{0}(q,p)+e{\phi}(q)

with the corresponding eigenprojections

P±​(q,p)=12​(1±1p0​(q,p)​(α⋅(p−ec​A​(q))+β​m​c)),P_{\pm}(q,p)=\frac{1}{2}\left(1\pm\frac{1}{p_{0}(q,p)}\left(\alpha\cdot\left(p-\frac{e}{c}A(q)\right)+\beta mc\right)\right)\,,

where p0​(q,p)=m2​c2+(p−ec​A​(q))2p_{0}(q,p)=\sqrt{m^{2}c^{2}+(p-\frac{e}{c}A(q))^{2}}. Obviously

E+​(q,p)−E−​(q,p)=2​c​p0​(q,p)≥C⁡⟨p⟩>0,E_{+}(q,p)-E_{-}(q,p)=2cp_{0}(q,p)\geq C\langle p\rangle>0\,,

whenever AA is uniformly bounded. Therefore the corresponding subspaces are adiabatically decoupled and the effective dynamics on each of them can be computed using our general scheme. Assuming A∈Cb∞​(ℝ3,ℝ3)A\in C_{\mathrm{b}}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R}^{3}) and ϕ∈Cb∞​(ℝ3,ℝ){\phi}\in C_{\mathrm{b}}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R}), one finds that H0∈S11H_{0}\in S_{1}^{1} and thus the assumptions from Section 2 are satisfied. In particular, H^D\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}} is essentially self-adjoint on 𝒮⁡(ℝ4,ℂ4)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4},\mathbb{C}^{4}) and E^±\widehat{E}_{\pm} on 𝒮⁡(ℝ4)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{4}).

To be consistent with the notation from the previous sections, let π0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p) =P+​(q,p)=P_{+}(q,p) be the projector on the electron band. The reference subspace for the electrons is 𝒦=L2​(ℝ3,ℂ2)\mathcal{K}=L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{2}) and it is convenient to define it as the range of

Πr:=(𝟏ℂ2000){\Pi_{\rm r}}:=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}&0\\ 0&0\end{array}\right)

in L2​(ℝ3,ℂ4)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{4}).

The only choice left is the one of u0​(q,p)u_{0}(q,p) or, equivalently, of a basis {ψα​(q,p)}α=1,2\{\psi_{\alpha}(q,p)\}_{\alpha=1,2} of Ranπ0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p). The eigenvectors ψ±​(q,p)\psi_{\pm}(q,p) of the operator e3⋅S⁡(q,p)e_{3}\cdot S(q,p) in Ranπ0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p) are

The relevant part of u0u_{0} for the analysis of the electron band is thus given by u0∗​(q,p)=(ψ+​(q,p),ψ−​(q,p)CLOSE,u_{0}^{*}(q,p)=\big(\psi_{+}(q,p),\psi_{-}(q,p), OPEN∗,∗)*,*\big) with u0∈S10u_{0}\in S_{1}^{0}. [FoWo], diagonalizes the free Dirac Hamiltonian H0​(p)H_{0}(p), i.e. HDH_{\mathrm{D}} with A,ϕ≡0A,{\phi}\equiv 0. For the subprincipal symbol after a lengthy but straightforward calculation our basic formula (37) yields

We summarize our results on the adiabatic decoupling and the effective dynamics for the Dirac equation in the following

Theorem 6.1.

Let A∈Cb∞​(ℝ3,ℝ3)A\in C_{\mathrm{b}}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R}^{3}) and ϕ∈Cb∞​(ℝ3,ℝ){\phi}\in C_{\mathrm{b}}^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{R}). In particular, he,1​(q,p)h_{\mathrm{e,1}}(q,p) is given by (67) and thus

h^e=(c​m2c2+(−iεℏ∇−ecA(x))2+e​ϕ​(q))​𝟏ℂ2−ε​ℏ2​σ⋅Ω⁡(q,p)^+𝒪0​(ε2).\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{e}}=\Big(c\sqrt{m^{2}c^{2}+(-i\varepsilon\hbar\nabla-\frac{e}{c}A(x))^{2}}+e{\phi}(q)\Big)\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}\,-\,\varepsilon\,\frac{\hbar}{2}\,\sigma\cdot\widehat{\Omega(q,p)}\,+\,\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{2})\,.

Analogous results hold for hph_{\mathrm{p}}. The errors in (70) and (6.1) are in the norm of bounded operators on L2​(ℝ3,ℂ4)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{4}), resp. on L2​(ℝ3,ℂ2)L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{3},\mathbb{C}^{2}).

According to the effective Hamiltonian (6.1) the gg-factor of the electron equals 22. There would be no problem to add to the Dirac Hamiltonian the standard subprincipal symbol [Th], which accounts for the slightly larger gg-factor of real electrons. Blount [Bl2] computes the second order effective Hamiltonian he,2h_{\rm e,2}, which he finds to be proportional to 𝟏ℂ2{\bf 1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}. he,2h_{\rm e,2} is a sum of terms allowed by dimensional reasoning, i.e. proportional to ∇B\nabla B, ∇E\nabla E, B2B^{2}, E2E^{2}, E​BEB. Second order corrections seem to be of interest for the dynamics of electrons in storage rings. Ignoring the contribution [Bl2], nonrigorous expansions are [DeKo] and [HeBa].

6.2 The semiclassical limit of the Dirac equation

Equipped with he,0h_{\rm e,0} and he,1h_{\rm e,1} we can apply the general results of Section 5 on the semiclassical limit to the Dirac equation. Let Φ±t\Phi_{\pm}^{t} be the Hamiltonian flows generated by E±​(q,p)E_{\pm}(q,p) on phase space ℝ6\mathbb{R}^{6} and let B^=b^​ 1\widehat{B}=\widehat{b}\,\mathbf{1}, b∈S10​(ℝ)b\in S_{1}^{0}(\mathbb{R}), be a semiclassical observable in the unrotated Hilbert space which does not depend on spin. From Corollary 5.2 we conclude for each T<∞T<\infty the existence of a constant CTC_{T} such that for all t∈[−T,T]t\in[-T,T]

‖(B⁡(t)−𝒲ε​(b⁡(Φ+t))​ 1)​Π+‖≤ε​CT,‖(B⁡(t)−𝒲ε​(b⁡(Φ−t))​ 1)​Π−‖≤ε​CT,\Big\|\Big(B(t)-\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}\big(b(\Phi_{+}^{t})\big)\,\mathbf{1}\Big)\Pi_{+}\Big\|\leq\,\varepsilon\,C_{T}\,,\,\,\Big\|\Big(B(t)-\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}\big(b(\Phi_{-}^{t})\big)\,\mathbf{1}\Big)\Pi_{-}\Big\|\leq\,\varepsilon\,C_{T}\,,

where B(t)=ei​H^D​t/(ε​ℏ)B^e−iH^Dt/(εℏ)B(t)=e^{i\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}}t/(\varepsilon\hbar)}\,\widehat{B}\,e^{-i\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}}t/(\varepsilon\hbar)}. Hence, to leading order, states in the range of Π+\Pi_{+} behave like classical relativistic electrons and states in the range of Π−\Pi_{-} like classical relativistic positrons. We emphasize that, in general, Π±\Pi_{\pm} are not spectral projections of H^D\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}}, since the variation of ϕ{\phi} can be larger than the mass gap 2​m​c22mc^{2}. Hence in the limit of slowly varying potentials a natural characterization of “electronic” and “positronic” subspaces is obtained which does not come from spectral projections of the free or full Dirac Hamiltonian.

Next we discuss the leading order spin dynamics, which in the first place requires to figure out which operator represents the spin of the electron. There has been a considerable discussion on this point, cf. [Th], with no general consensus reached. We suspect that the problem is void. The wave function is spinor valued and what is observed is the spatial splitting of different spinor components in inhomogeneous magnetic fields. Hence we should pick the “spin observable” Σ\Sigma such that the splitting can nicely be attributed to it. E.g., in a magnetic field with gradient along the zz-direction the eigenvectors of Σz\Sigma_{z} should have the property that their spatial support goes either parallel to +z+z or to −z-z, but should not split. In view of (6.1) a natural choice is to take as spin operator the vector of Pauli-matrices σ\sigma in the rotated electronic subspace. In the original Hilbert space this amounts to

Σ=U∗​(σ00σ)​U=2ℏ​S^+𝒪⁡(ε),\Sigma=U^{*}\,\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}\sigma&0\\ 0&\sigma\end{array}\right)\,U=\frac{2}{\hbar}\,\widehat{S}+\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon)\,,

where S⁡(q,p)S(q,p) is the “mean” spin defined before.

The leading order semiclassical approximation for

σ(t)=ei​h^e​t/(ε​ℏ)σe−ih^et/(εℏ)\sigma(t)=e^{i\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{e}}t/(\varepsilon\hbar)}\,\sigma\,e^{-i\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{e}}t/(\varepsilon\hbar)}

follows from Theorem 5.1. For each T<∞T<\infty there is a constant CT<∞C_{T}<\infty such that for t∈[−T,T]t\in[-T,T]

‖σ⁡(t)−σ0​(t)^‖≤ε​CT,\big\|\sigma(t)-\widehat{\sigma_{0}(t)}\big\|\leq\,\varepsilon\,C_{T}\,, (71)

where σ0​k​(q,p,t)\sigma_{0k}(q,p,t), k∈{1,2,3}k\in\{1,2,3\}, is obtained as the solution of

∂σ0​k​(q,p,t)∂t=−i2​[σ⋅Ω⁡(Φ+t​(q,p)),σ0​k​(q,p,t)]\frac{\partial\,\sigma_{0k}(q,p,t)}{\partial t}=-\,\frac{i}{2}\,\Big[\,\sigma\cdot\Omega(\Phi_{+}^{t}(q,p)),\,\sigma_{0k}(q,p,t)\,\Big] (72)

with initial condition σ0​k​(q,p,0)=σk\sigma_{0k}(q,p,0)=\sigma_{k}. This follows from the Equations (54) and (55) by setting σ0​k​(q,p,t)=D∗​(q,p,t)​σk​D​(q,p,t)\sigma_{0k}(q,p,t)=D^{*}(q,p,t)\,\sigma_{k}\,D(q,p,t).

To solve Equation (72) one makes an ansatz σ0​k​(q,p,t)=sk​(q,p,t)⋅σ\sigma_{0k}(q,p,t)=s_{k}(q,p,t)\cdot\sigma with sk​(q,p,0)=eks_{k}(q,p,0)=e_{k}. Using [σn,σm]=2​i​εn​m​k​σk[\sigma_{n},\sigma_{m}]=2\,i\,\varepsilon_{nmk}\,\sigma_{k}, one finds that the spin- or “magnetization”-vector sk​(q,p,t)s_{k}(q,p,t) is given as the solution of

∂sk​(q,p,t)∂t=−sk​(q,p,t)∧Ω⁡(Φ+t​(q,p)).\frac{\partial\,s_{k}(q,p,t)}{\partial t}=-\,s_{k}(q,p,t)\,\wedge\,\Omega(\Phi_{+}^{t}(q,p))\,. (73)

(73) is the BMT-equation [BMT, Ja] on the level of observables. It was derived by Bargmann, Michel and Telegdi in 1959 on purely classical grounds as the simplest Lorentz invariant equation for the spin dynamics of a classical relativistic particle.

The semiclassical limit of the Dirac equation has been discussed repeatedly and we mention only some recent work. Yajima [Ya] considers time-dependent external fields and proves directly a semiclassical expansion for the corresponding propagator. As mentioned already at the end of Section 5, this program is mathematically rather involved, since one faces the problem of caustics in the classical flow, and different expansions have to be glued together in order to obtain results valid for all macroscopic times. Based on the same approach Bolte and Keppeler [BoKe2] derive a Gutzwiller type trace formula. Since H^D\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}} and U∗​H^D​UU^{*}\,\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}}\,U are isospectral and since (70) holds, a trace formula for the eigenvalue statistics of H^D\widehat{H}_{\mathrm{D}} could as well be derived from the semiclassical propagator of h^=h^e⊗𝟏+𝟏⊗h^p\widehat{h}=\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{e}}\otimes\mathbf{1}+\mathbf{1}\otimes\widehat{h}_{\mathrm{p}}. As argued in Section 5, the latter is somewhat easier to obtain. In [GMMP, Sp] the semiclassical limit of the Dirac equation is discussed using matrix-valued Wigner functions. Their results hold for an arbitrary macroscopic time interval, but fuse, as does the WKB approach, adiabatic and semiclassical limit. No higher order corrections seem to be accessible and the results are weaker than ours in the sense that the approximations do not hold uniformly in the states.

This leads us to the next natural question: What can be said about higher order corrections? While in general one would need he,2h_{\rm e,2}, according to (52) the semiclassical limit of observables of the type b^=b^0​𝟏ℂ2\widehat{b}=\widehat{b}_{0}\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}}, b0∈S10​(ℝ)b_{0}\in S^{0}_{1}(\mathbb{R}), can be determined without this explicit information. For such a scalar symbol the principal symbol b0​(t)b_{0}(t), i.e. the solution to (51), will remain scalar and thus its commutator with he,2h_{\mathrm{e,2}} in (52) vanishes identically for all times. The solution b1​(t)b_{1}(t) of (52) with initial condition b1​(0)=0b_{1}(0)=0, is not scalar, in general. Hence, at this order there is back reaction of the spin dynamics on the translational motion. We illustrate this point for the position operator x⁡(q,p)=x0​(q,p):=q​ 1ℂ2x(q,p)=x_{0}(q,p):=q\,\mathbf{1}_{\mathbb{C}^{2}} and refer to [Te3] for a general analysis of the higher order effects in the semiclassical dynamics of Dirac particles. Now x0​(q,p,t)=x0​(Φ+t​(q,p))x_{0}(q,p,t)=x_{0}\big(\Phi^{t}_{+}(q,p)\big) and x1​(t)x_{1}(t) is obtained, according to Equation (52), as the solution of

d​x1​(t)d​t={E+​𝟏,x1​(t)}+i⁡[he,1,x1​(t)]−{he,1,x0​(t)}\frac{d\,x_{1}(t)}{dt}=\{E_{+}\mathbf{1},x_{1}(t)\}+i[h_{\mathrm{e,1}},x_{1}(t)]-\{h_{\mathrm{e,1}},x_{0}(t)\} (74)

with initial condition x1​(0)=0x_{1}(0)=0. The homogeneous part of this equation is just the classical translational and spin motion and the inhomogeneity is

{he,1,x0(t)}=−ℏ2σ⋅{Ω,x0(t)},\{h_{\mathrm{e,1}},x_{0}(t)\}=-\frac{\hbar}{2}\,\sigma\cdot\{\,\Omega,x_{0}(t)\}\,, (75)

which is not scalar and thus responsible for the splitting of trajectories of electrons with distinct spin orientation. Hence, as in (58),

x1(t)=−ℏ2∫0tds𝒰(t−s)σ⋅{Ω,x0(s)},x_{1}(t)=-\frac{\hbar}{2}\int_{0}^{t}\,ds\,\mathcal{U}(t-s)\,\sigma\cdot\{\,\Omega,\,x_{0}(s)\}\,,

where 𝒰⁡(t)\mathcal{U}(t) is the “classical flow” defined through (56).

Without claim of rigor, we observe in (68) that for small velocities v⁡(q,p)v(q,p) one has

Ω⁡(q,p)≈em​c​B​(q).\Omega(q,p)\approx\frac{e}{mc}\,B(q)\,.

Let us further assume that B⁡(q)=b​qz​ezB(q)=b\,q_{z}\,e_{z}, then

ℏ2​σ⋅{Ω,x0​(t)}=ℏ​e2​m​c​σz​∂B∂qz​∂Φqt∂pz=t​ℏ​e2​m2​c​(b00−b)\frac{\hbar}{2}\,\sigma\cdot\{\Omega,x_{0}(t)\}=\frac{\hbar e}{2mc}\sigma_{z}\frac{\partial B}{\partial q_{z}}\,\frac{\partial\Phi_{q}^{t}}{\partial p_{z}}=t\,\frac{\hbar e}{2m^{2}c}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}b&0\\ 0&-b\end{array}\right)

and thus according to (74), (75) the correction to the velocity is proportional to tt, corresponding to a constant force with absolute value ℏ​e/(2​m​c)​|∇B|\hbar e/(2mc)|\nabla B|, as expected for a spin-12\frac{1}{2} particle.

7 Conclusions

The basic formulae (33), (34) can be applied, in essence in a mechanical fashion, to any concrete quantum problem with two provisos. First of all the problem has to be cast into the general form (1) and secondly one must have sufficient information on the principal symbol H0​(q,p)H_{0}(q,p). Depending on H0H_{0} considerable simplifications of (33), (34) may be in force, one example being the effective Hamiltonian of the time-adiabatic theorem studied in Section 4.4. As a net result, if the conditions of the space-adiabatic Theorem 2.1 are satisfied, the full Schrödinger equation is approximated by an effective Schrödinger equation referring to a specific relevant energy band. The errors are estimated and, in general, the time scale of validity is much larger than the one which can be reached within a semiclassical approximation.

We focused our interest on a single relevant energy band. No information on the complement is needed except for global quantities like the resolvent (H0​(q,p)−Er​(q,p))−1​(1−π0​(q,p))(H_{0}(q,p)-{E_{\rm r}}(q,p))^{-1}(1-\pi_{0}(q,p)). In previous investigations [Bl1, LiFl] all energy bands are treated simultaneously. An example which would not fall under such a scheme is nonrelativistic QED, which governs electrons coupled to the quantized radiation field. In this case the principal symbol has a two-fold degenerate eigenvalue at the bottom of the spectrum separated by a gap from the continuous spectrum, provided |p||p| is sufficiently small and there is a suitable infrared cutoff [PST1].

The main restriction of our work is the gap condition of Section 2. There are two standard mechanisms of how this condition is violated. (1) There are two (or possibly more) locally isolated energy bands of constant multiplicity which cross on a lower dimensional submanifold. Away from the crossing region the wave function in one band is governed by the effective Hamiltonian discussed before. If the wave function comes close to the crossing manifold, there is a certain probability to make a transition to the other band. In rather specific model systems such transitions have been studied in considerable detail [Ha2, HaJo1, FeGe, FeLa]. (2) H0H_{0} has a smooth band of constant multiplicity bordering the continuous spectrum without gap. This is the rule in models from nonrelativistic QED with massless photons. Results for the massless Nelson model [Te1] indicate that smoothness of π0​(q,p)\pi_{0}(q,p) suffices also in general for adiabatic decoupling at leading order with intraband dynamics generated by h0+ε​h1h_{0}+\varepsilon h_{1} as defined by (36). However, the expansion stops at this stage. Physically, the electron looses energy through radiation, which means that the next order correction must be dissipative.

¿From the physics point of view the dynamics of molecules and the dynamics of electrons in a solid are the two most prominent areas of application for the space-adiabatic perturbation theory. The former has been discussed already in Section 4.3. Bloch electrons do not quite fall into our scheme, since the classical phase space is ℝd×𝕋d\mathbb{R}^{d}\times\mathbb{T}^{d}, 𝕋d\mathbb{T}^{d} a flat dd-dimensional torus. This requires substantial changes which are discussed in [PST2].

Appendix A Operator-valued Weyl calculus

Pseudodifferential operators with operator-valued symbols have been widely discussed in the literature. The results presented in this Appendix can be found in [Hö, Fo, Iv, GMS]. We start with some notation. Let ℰ\mathcal{E} be a Banach space, then 𝒞⁡(ℝd,ℰ)\mathcal{C}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{E}) denote the space of ℰ\mathcal{E}-valued continuous functions on ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d}. In the same spirit we will employ the notation 𝒮⁡(ℝd,ℰ)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{E}), Lp​(ℝd,ℰ)L^{p}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{E}), with the obvious meaning. Note that, in the special case where ℰ=ℋf\mathcal{E=H}_{\rm f} is an Hilbert space, one has L2​(ℝd,ℋf)≅L2​(ℝd)⊗ℋfL^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\rm f})\cong L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d})\otimes\mathcal{H}_{\rm f}. The space of the bounded operators on ℰ\mathcal{E} will be denoted as ℬ⁡(ℰ)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{E}).

A.1 Weyl quantization

Let AA be a ℬ⁡(ℋf)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})-valued rapidly decreasing smooth function on ℝ2​d\mathbb{R}^{2d}, i.e. A∈𝒮⁡(ℝ2​d,ℬ⁡(ℋf))A\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{2d},\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})). If we denote by ℱ​A\mathcal{F}A the Fourier transform of AA then, by Fourier inversion formula,

A⁡(q,p)=1(2​π)d​∫ℝ2​d(ℱ​A)​(η,ξ)​ei⁡(η⋅q+ξ⋅p)​𝑑η​𝑑ξ,A(q,p)=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}(\mathcal{F}A)(\eta,\xi)\ e^{i(\eta\cdot q+\xi\cdot p)}\ d\eta d\xi\,,

(ei⁡(η⋅q^+ξ⋅p^)​ψ)​(x)=ei​ε​(η⋅ξ)/2​ei​η⋅x​ψ​(x+ε​ξ)for ​ψ∈L2​(ℝd).\left(e^{i(\eta\cdot\widehat{q}+\xi\cdot\widehat{p})}\psi\right)(x)=e^{i\varepsilon(\eta\cdot\xi)/2}e^{i\eta\cdot x}\psi(x+\varepsilon\xi)\qquad\mbox{for }\psi\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d}). (76)

Thus

A^=1(2​π)d​∫ℝ2​d(ℱ​A)​(η,ξ)​(ei⁡(η⋅q^+ξ⋅p^)⊗1ℋf)​𝑑η​𝑑ξ,\widehat{A}=\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}(\mathcal{F}A)(\eta,\xi)\ \left(e^{i(\eta\cdot\widehat{q}+\xi\cdot\widehat{p})}\otimes 1_{\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}}\right)d\eta d\xi\,, (77)

and, in particular,

‖A^‖ℬ⁡(ℋ)≤1(2​π)d​∫ℝ2​d‖(ℱ​A)​(η,ξ)‖ℬ⁡(ℋf)​𝑑η​𝑑ξ,\big\|\widehat{A}\big\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})}\leq\frac{1}{(2\pi)^{d}}\int_{\mathbb{R}^{2d}}\left\|(\mathcal{F}A)(\eta,\xi)\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})}\ d\eta d\xi\,,

Substituting (76) in (77) one obtains that for every ψ∈𝒮⁡(ℝd,ℋf)\psi\in\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})

Definition A.1.

A function A∈C∞​(ℝ2​d,ℬ⁡(ℋf))A\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}^{2d},\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) belongs to the symbol class Sρm​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))S_{\rho}^{m}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) ((with m∈ℝm\in\mathbb{R} and 𝑂𝑃𝐸𝑁0≤ρ≤1)0\leq\rho\leq 1) if for every α,β∈ℕd\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{N}^{d} there exists a positive constant Cα,βC_{\alpha,\beta} such that

supq∈ℝd‖(∂qα∂pβA)​(q,p)‖ℬ⁡(ℋf)≤Cα,β​⟨p⟩m−ρ​|β|\sup_{q\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\|(\partial_{q}^{\alpha}\partial_{p}^{\beta}A)(q,p)\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})}\leq C_{\alpha,\beta}\ \left\langle p\right\rangle^{m-\rho|\beta|}

‖A‖k(m)=sup|α|+|β|≤ksupq,p∈ℝd⟨p⟩−m+ρ​|β|​‖(∂qα∂pβA)​(q,p)‖ℬ⁡(ℋf),k∈ℕ.\left\|A\right\|_{k}^{(m)}=\sup_{|\alpha|+|\beta|\leq k}\sup_{q,p\in\mathbb{R}^{d}}\left\langle p\right\rangle^{-m+\rho|\beta|}\left\|(\partial_{q}^{\alpha}\partial_{p}^{\beta}A)(q,p)\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})}\,,\qquad k\in\mathbb{N}\,. (79)

The following result is proved exactly as in the scalar case, cf. also [GMS].

Proposition A.2.

Let A∈Sρm​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))A\in S^{m}_{\rho}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\rm f})), then A^\widehat{A} given trough (78) maps 𝒮⁡(ℝd,ℋf)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\rm f}) continuously into itself.

A.2 The Weyl-Moyal product

Next we consider the composition of symbols. The behavior of the symbol classes with respect to the pointwise product is very simple, as can be proved by using the Leibniz rule.

Proposition A.4.

If AA ∈Sρm1​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))\in S_{\rho}^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) and B∈Sρm2​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))B\in S_{\rho}^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})), then A​BAB belongs to
Sρm1+m2​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))S_{\rho}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) for every m1,m2∈ℝm_{1},m_{2}\in\mathbb{R}.

The behavior under pointwise inversion is described in the following proposition. For every T∈ℬ⁡(ℋf)T\in\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}) let the internal spectral radius be ρint​(T):=inf{|λ|:λ∈σ⁡(T)}.\rho_{\mathrm{int}}(T):=\inf\left\{|\lambda|:\lambda\in\sigma(T)\right\}.

ρint​(A⁡(q,p))≥C0​⟨p⟩mfor any ​p∈ℝd.\rho_{\mathrm{int}}(A(q,p))\geq C_{0}\left\langle p\right\rangle^{m}\qquad\mbox{for any }\,\,p\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\,.

‖∇p(A−1)‖ℬ⁡(ℋf)=‖−A−1​(∇pA)​A−1‖ℬ⁡(ℋf)≤C′​⟨p⟩−m−ρ\left\|\nabla_{p}(A^{-1})\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})}=\left\|-A^{-1}(\nabla_{p}A)\ A^{-1}\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})}\leq C^{\prime}\left\langle p\right\rangle^{-m-\rho}

and applying the chain rule. ∎

The crucial result for pseudodiferential calculus is the following. One can define an associative product in the space of classical symbols which corresponds to the composition of the operators. Given A∈Sρm1​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))A\in S_{\rho}^{m_{1}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) and B∈Sρm2​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))B\in S_{\rho}^{m_{2}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) we know that A^\widehat{A} and B^\widehat{B} map 𝒮⁡(ℝd,ℋf)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}) into itself. Then A^​B^\widehat{A}\widehat{B} is still an operator on 𝒮⁡(ℝd,ℋf)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}) and one can show that there exists a unique ε\varepsilon-dependent symbol Symb⁡(A^​B^)=:A​#~​B∈Sρm1+m2​(ℬ⁡(ℋf)){\rm Symb}({\widehat{A}\widehat{B}})=:A\,\tilde{\#}\,B\in S_{\rho}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})) such that

𝒲ε​(A)​𝒲ε​(B)=𝒲ε​(A​#~​B)​. \mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}(A)\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}(B)=\mathcal{W}_{\varepsilon}(A\ \tilde{\#}\ B)\mbox{. }

Since the product A​#~​BA\ \tilde{\#}\ B depends on ε\varepsilon by construction, one can expand (80) in orders of ε\varepsilon. To this end, it is convenient to define suitable classes of ε\varepsilon-dependent symbols, called semiclassical symbols, which – roughly speaking – are close to a power series in ε\varepsilon of classical symbols with nicer and nicer behavior at infinity. Our definition is a special case of the standard ones (see [DiSj, Ma, Fo, Hö]).

As a consequence of the previous result, it is convenient to introduce the space of the formal power series with coefficients in Sρ∞​(ℬ⁡(ℋf))S_{\rho}^{\infty}(\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})). In particular we will denote as Mρm​(ε)M_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon) the subspace of the formal power series with a resummation in Sρm​(ε)S_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon), i.e.

Mρm​(ε):={∑j≥0εj​Aj:Aj∈Sρm−j​ρ}.M_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon):=\left\{\sum_{j\geq 0}\varepsilon^{j}A_{j}:A_{j}\in S_{\rho}^{m-j\rho}\right\}\,.

In the context of formal power series, the product defined by (82) will be called the Moyal product and denoted simply as #\# . Notice that #\# defines a map from Mρm1​(ε)×Mρm2​(ε)M_{\rho}^{m_{1}}(\varepsilon)\times M_{\rho}^{m_{2}}(\varepsilon) to Mρm1+m2​(ε)M_{\rho}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\varepsilon). The Moyal product can also be regarded as a map from Mρm1​(ε,ℬ⁡(ℋf))×Mρm2​(ε,ℋf)M_{\rho}^{m_{1}}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}))\times M_{\rho}^{m_{2}}(\varepsilon,\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}) to Mρm1+m2​(ℋf)M_{\rho}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}), where in (82) the operator AA and its derivatives act on the vector BB and its derivatives.

To sum up the previous discussion, we wish to point out that one can prove statements on three levels: formal symbols (i.e. formal power series), semiclassical symbols, and operators on 𝒮⁡(ℝd,ℋf)⊆L2​(ℝd,ℋf)\mathcal{S}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}})\subseteq L^{2}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}). A simple example illustrates the interplay between these levels. Suppose that two formal symbols A∈Mρm1​(ε)A\in M_{\rho}^{m_{1}}(\varepsilon) and B∈Mρm2​(ε)B\in M_{\rho}^{m_{2}}(\varepsilon) Moyal commute, i.e. [A,B]#=A​#​B−B​#​A=0[A,B]_{\#}=A\#B-B\#A=0. Let Aε∈Sρm1​(ε)A_{\varepsilon}\in S_{\rho}^{m_{1}}(\varepsilon) and Bε∈Sρm2​(ε)B_{\varepsilon}\in S_{\rho}^{m_{2}}(\varepsilon) be any two resummations of AA and, respectively, BB. Since we know a priori (by Prop. A.9) that the Weyl product Aε​#~​BεA_{\varepsilon}\ \tilde{\#}\ B_{\varepsilon} belongs to Sρm1+m2​(ε)S_{\rho}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\varepsilon) it follows that the Weyl commutator [Aε,Bε]#~[A_{\varepsilon},B_{\varepsilon}]_{\tilde{\#}} is asymptotically close to zero in Sρm1+m2​(ε)S_{\rho}^{m_{1}+m_{2}}(\varepsilon), which can be rephrased in the following way: for any n,k∈ℕn,k\in\mathbb{N} there exists a constant Cn,kC_{n,k} such that for any ε∈[0,ε0)\varepsilon\in[0,\varepsilon_{0}) one has

‖[Aε,Bε]#~‖k(m1+m2−n​ρ)≤Cn,k​εn.\left\|[A_{\varepsilon},B_{\varepsilon}]_{\tilde{\#}}\right\|_{k}^{(m_{1}+m_{2}-n\rho)}\leq C_{n,k}\ \varepsilon^{n}\,.

If ρ>0\rho>0 we obtain that definitely m1+m2−n​ρ≤0m_{1}+m_{2}-n\rho\leq 0 for some n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and then Prop. A.3 assures that the operator commutator [A^ε,B^ε][\widehat{A}_{\varepsilon},\widehat{B}_{\varepsilon}] can be bounded in the ℬ⁡(ℋ)\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})-norm. Moreover, for ρ>0\rho>0, we can conclude that [A^ε,B^ε][\widehat{A}_{\varepsilon},\widehat{B}_{\varepsilon}] is a smoothing operator (i.e. it belongs to OPSρ−∞:=∩m∈ℝOPSρmOPS_{\rho}^{-\infty}:=\cap_{m\in\mathbb{R}}OPS_{\rho}^{m}) and in particular one can prove that it is a “small” bounded operator between the Sobolev spaces HqH^{q} and Hq+rH^{q+r} for any q,r∈ℕq,r\in\mathbb{N}. To be precise, for any q,r,n∈ℕq,r,n\in\mathbb{N} there exist a constant Cn,q,rC_{n,q,r} such that

‖[A^ε,B^ε]‖ℬ⁡(Hq,Hq+r)≤Cn,q,r​εn\left\|[\widehat{A}_{\varepsilon},\widehat{B}_{\varepsilon}]\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(H^{q},H^{q+r})}\leq C_{n,q,r}\,\varepsilon^{n}

for any ε∈[0,ε0)\varepsilon\in[0,\varepsilon_{0}), where HqH^{q} stands for Hq​(ℝd,ℋf)H^{q}(\mathbb{R}^{d},\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{f}}). Notice that for ρ=0\rho=0 and m1+m2=:m>0m_{1}+m_{2}=:m>0 it is not possible to conclude from [A,B]#=0[A,B]_{\#}=0 that [A^ε,B^ε][\widehat{A}_{\varepsilon},\widehat{B}_{\varepsilon}] is a bounded operator, since it could happen – for example – that [Aε,Bε]#~=e−1ε​pm,[A_{\varepsilon},B_{\varepsilon}]_{\tilde{\#}}=e^{-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}}p^{m}, which is asymptotically close to zero in Sρm​(ε)S_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon). In the following we will use the same symbol for an element in Sρm​(ε)S^{m}_{\rho}(\varepsilon) and its expansion in Mρm​(ε)M^{m}_{\rho}(\varepsilon). As suggested by the preceding discussion, we introduce the following synthetic notation.

Notation. Let be AA and BB semiclassical symbols in Sρm​(ε)S_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon). We will say that B=A+𝒪−∞​(ε∞)B=A+\mathcal{O}_{-\infty}(\varepsilon^{\infty}) if B−AB-A is asymptotically close to zero in Sρm​(ε)S_{\rho}^{m}(\varepsilon) for ρ>0\rho>0.

With a little abuse, we will employ the same notation for pseudodifferential operators too, i.e. we write B^=A^+𝒪−∞​(ε∞)\widehat{B}=\widehat{A}+\mathcal{O}_{-\infty}(\varepsilon^{\infty}) if B=A+𝒪−∞​(ε∞)B=A+\mathcal{O}_{-\infty}(\varepsilon^{\infty}). As noticed above this is a strong concept of closeness, since it implies that B^−A^\widehat{B}-\widehat{A} is a smoothing operator. Compare with the following weaker concept.

Notation. Let be RR and SS two (ε\varepsilon-dependent) operators on ℋ\mathcal{H}. We will say that R=S+𝒪0​(ε∞)R=S+\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty}) if for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} there exists a constant CnC_{n} such that

‖R−S‖ℬ⁡(ℋ)≤Cn​εn\left\|R-S\right\|_{\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})}\leq C_{n}\varepsilon^{n}

for every ε∈[0,ε0)\varepsilon\in[0,\varepsilon_{0}). In such a case we will say that RR is 𝒪0​(ε∞)\mathcal{O}_{0}(\varepsilon^{\infty})-close to SS.
